speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) asked for information regarding channel depths between the Welland canal and the head of the lakes. I told him I would get that information for him. Since I believe there is general interest in this matter, I should like to give a very brief report now.
The United States corps of engineers continues to assume responsibility for the deepening in the channels upstream from the Welland canal. The limiting depth from the Welland canal to lake Superior is 21 feet in the upbound channel at Amherstburg; the downbound channel at that point has a depth of 25 feet. The Detroit river dredging is expected to be completed in 1960 to a depth of 25 feet, which will provide a draft of 23 feet.
Dredging is in progress in the St. Mary's river, but until completion about 1962, the existing depth of 21 feet for upbound navigation and 25 feet for downbound navigation will remain in effect. The deepening to regular seaway standards-that is, over-all depth to 27 feet-is scheduled for 1963 in all channels.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I never anticipated that it would take me two days to deliver my maiden speech.
At this time I should like to join in the welcome that has been extended to our two distinguished guests from other nations of the commonwealth who are visiting us today. I hope their stay here will prove to be as rewarding and educational as it has proven entertaining.
Last night at the hour of adjournment I had disposed of that part of my speech in which I dealt with the position of the opposition. I had gone on to outline some of the great challenges we face in the world today. 1 discussed the great demand for qualified and dedicated leadership. Of what does leadership consist? The greatness of a leader lies in his dignity, his diplomacy and his belief in democracy. Dignity consists of simplicity, sincerity and seriousness of purpose. Diplomacy consists of the ability to respect the other person's point of view, the ability to reason and the ability to co-operate.
In brief, democracy consists of the fundamental freedoms; freedom to believe, freedom to speak those beliefs; freedom of the press to perpetuate and criticize those beliefs. There is also freedom from fear of persecution for your views; that is, the right to be wrong. I suggest that this last is the most important for without it the others perish. More recently a new freedom has evolved, freedom from want, and we all subscribe to it to a degree. However, when economic

The Address-Mr. Houck freedom is overextended it tends to infringe on political freedom. There is a danger of drifting in that direction today. Economic freedom versus political freedom is the biggest issue of the day and one that will hold the stage for many decades to come. We must find a formula of the relativity of the two that is consistent with the principles of democracy.
Just as there is a demand for leadership, there is a demand on leadership. A leader must be prepared to give far more than he will ever receive, for leadership is a life of selflessness, service and sacrifice. High as are the qualifications of leadership that I have outlined there are, I submit, hon. gentlemen in this chamber who meet those qualifications. But I would also submit that there is one man who meets those qualifications in an outstanding manner and his name, like that of Abou ben Adhem, leads all the rest. I refer to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
To hon. members of this house of all parties may I say this, Mr. Speaker. All of us have a great heritage to which we must live up, and as individuals we should stand for principles we know are right. There is a great challenge before us. As individuals we should not bow before overbearing majorities or vociferous minorities whoever they may be. Nor should we yield to the defeatist cry that "It can't be done". That cry has re-echoed on Canada's frontiers in the past, when it could be done and was done. Our people place in us their faith and hope for peace and progress. It seems to me that all of us in this chamber are pressing our shoulders to that great wheel which turns the gears of democracy and leads to progress. I am sure that somewhere in that great book in which the annals of Canadian history are written each one will make his little mark with a job well done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the very outset may I say that one returns to a new session of parliament with mingled feelings. One experiences a sense of anticipation, looking forward to meeting various members of parliament in sincere friendship and wondering how they are faring in their individual ridings. But one is also touched with deep regret when one learns, as generally happens, that we are called upon to pay our respects to a few of our number who have been called to their great reward.
I believe we also return with a feeling of anxiety about what the speech from the throne is going to contain. To the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne may I repeat what has been said

so well on many previous occasions. I felt they brought honour not only to themselves but to the party they represent and to the House of Commons as well in the fine and masterful way they talked about this speech that contained so little about which one could talk.
I also want to say, and I say this seriously indeed, that I extend a hearty and warm welcome to the new members of this house. Unfortunately our party did not fare too well in terms of strengthening its representation in this chamber, but I was especially glad to welcome to our midst the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who has a wealth of experience in parliamentary procedure and who will contribute much from his vast experience and ability.
I also wish to extend a sincere welcome to the hon. lady who represents the riding of Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman). I say that because I have always had a soft spot in my heart for her father, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe), with whom I have enjoyed a warm friendship extending over many years. He and I have in common something which is not shared by many other hon. members in this house, in that we both were born in the Unted States, and this has served to draw us together more closely than the reins of his race horses.
I hope it will be of interest to hon. members if I devote some time reporting to the house about the recent meeting in Washington of the joint Canada-United States interparliamentary committee. I feel I owe it to the house to report about our meeting. Before doing so, however, I want to say a hearty word of thanks not only to the Prime Minister but to my leader for honouring me by allowing me to serve on the committee. This was not only an honour to me but to the riding of Niagara Falls which I have the honour to represent, and the people of that area accepted it as such.
A few weeks ago, as hon. members will recall, some of us had the honour to serve on a committee appointed by this house to meet with a similar committee from the house of representatives of the United States to discuss important problems of mutual concern respecting our two great countries. It might be amusing to hon. gentlemen to know that at our very first meeting we discussed the proper name for this body. There were many good suggestions made, and after they were all taken and shuffled we finally decided and had rather a small baptismal service- that the committee be christened the Canada-United States interparliamentary group.
I wish to say that I was proud of our speaker in Washington and proud of the speaker of the other place as well because

of the leadership they gave us, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) so well said the other day. I can say this, Mr. Speaker, that in the limited experience I have had-and I know I am speaking the thoughts of the other members of the committee-we never experienced such wonderful hospitality as we met when we arrived and during our stay in Washington. I pay my utmost respect, and I find it rather difficult to find words adequately to express our sincere appreciation, to our embassy in Washington. I am so glad the Prime Minister has seen fit finally to appoint our ambassador to Washington, but his aides down there were performing a wonderful job. On leaving there I felt that they had left nothing undone that could have been done for our enjoyment. I think they are servants of whom we in Canada can be justly proud.
I also wish to say a word in regard to Mr. Merchant, who most hon. members know very well. He was formerly ambassador from the United States to Canada and now serves as undersecretary of state of the United States. I wish to thank him for the wonderful reception he and his wife gave to our committee. I was so glad we were allowed to take our wives along. I doubt, Mr. Speaker, whether the United States ever saw any better looking women than we had with us on that day. One of the highlights was that we were allowed to go to the White House and meet the President of the United States. It was a wonderful reception. We were invited into his office. He shook hands with each one personally; then he talked to us off the cuff, if I may use the expression, for about 10 minutes, and then he posed for a picture at his desk with our visiting Canadian group and before we left he shook hands with each one again.
I want to say that was one of the thrills of our meeting. He said then, and I noticed he used it in his speech to the nation, and these words will always stay with me in regard to our group visiting Washington; and I think it well for us to follow this on our side: "One basic purpose unites us; to promote strength and security side by side with liberty and opportunity."
Perhaps hon. members would like to know the composition of the committee. I shall go over it very quickly. First there was the Speaker of the other place, Senator William R. Brunt from Hanover and Senator Sydney John Smith from Kamloops. From this house we had our own esteemed Speaker and the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the
The Address-Mr. Houck hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Thrasher) and myself. We felt honoured to act on that committee.
Why was there such a committee? Why did the Prime Minister see fit to appoint such a committee, and why did the house discuss at no great length last session the formation of such a committee to meet with our friends to the south of us? May I put on record what some of the United States senators had to say? This is what Senator George Aiken from Vermont, one of the older senators, a very fine man, chairman of that committee, performing a wonderful job not only on behalf of his state but on behalf of the United States, had to say:
Reports of friction are exaggerated. Areas of agreement and co-operation are far more numerous than areas of disagreement.
Senator Richard Neuberger of Oregon, who was not on the committee, said:
Relationships have worsened during the past year because of needless irritations over tariffs, world wheat markets, mutual use of the upper Columbia river and similar problems. Canadians have exaggerated the degree to which their pride in national growth must be turned against the United States: this may have been agitated during the last Canadian election. Relationships could be improved by a plan for gradual elimination of all tariff barriers over a five-year period.
Senator Warren Magnuson of Washington said:
Relations slipped badly last year but Canada and the United States reassessed their stand. As a result relations are now on upturn.
Representative Frank Boykin of Alabama said:
Our relations did deteriorate during the past 12 months but are now on upswing.
Representative Sam Rayburn from Texas is certainly a man about whom we read in the press. He continues to be one of the finest men in the House of Representatives. Indeed, he could have had the nomination for President of the United States at different times, but he said, "If I had taken nomination for the presidency of the United States I would be out of a job at the present time." He has been Speaker of the House of Representatives for many years, and to know him is to appreciate him. He said:
Our relations are good because they must be.
Truer words were never spoken, Mr. Speaker. He said:
I expect to do everything I can to keep them on the highest level.
Representative Henry Reuss of Wisconsin said:
Slightly improved. Biggest single factor was the passage by congress of an amendment that requires our surplus disposal program to be so administered as not to interfere with the marketings of free countries. This would alleviate displacement of Canada's wheat exports.

The Address-Mr. Houck
I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that one could not help believing that those business meetings we had with representatives of the United States opened a new chapter of splendid friendship pertaining to Canadian-United States relations.
We decided at the meeting-and I think this will be of interest to all members of the house-that in addition to our committee of nine we would ask this house, and the United States committee agreed with this- to permit at future meetings 15 to 24 members of the house to accompany the committee. We decided that we would not necessarily hold all the meetings in Washington and Ottawa. We felt that if we had something to discuss with the United States about the Columbia river or some British Columbia problem it would be only right that we should go to British Columbia. United States representatives felt that if it was something having to do with the western United States it would be well for the committee to travel out to the western part of the United States.
I think it was a good thing that the committee felt that all hon. members should have the same status and the same opportunity as the regular members of the committee, and that they should be permitted to take part in discussions as well. Therefore when we have our next meeting I hope we shall have other hon. members with us. If we go to Quebec I hope we shall have Quebec members accompanying us.
Then we discussed the time and place of the next meeting. We decided we should meet at least twice a year. We decided that our meetings would be absolutely informal. Although we felt we could not bring forward any definite resolutions at the present time -that rests with the higher levels of government-we felt we could at least make recommendations and give some advice to the higher levels of government, and we thought that would be a good step toward the solution of some of our problems.
We decided that our next meeting would be in June, to correspond with the official opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. We would also like the members of the United States Senate and House of Representatives to be here while our house and Senate are still in session so they can see how we act here and, if possible, witness the prorogation of parliament. We also decided that, if possible, the committee should not only visit Ottawa and the St. Lawrence but we would take the members to various parts of Quebec as well as having them sail the length of the Welland canal and, of course, we would never overlook having them spend a day in Niagara Falls.

We decided that at the next meeting we would discuss certain problems. We had a round table discussion, and each member put forward what he thought would be the most important problems to discuss. The problems that were put on the next agenda were, first, defence relationships, and then trade problems, boundary water issues, water disposal, investment policies, revival of the Hyde Park agreement, fisheries problems, defence production questions and the co-ordination of Canadian and United States foreign policies.
When the opening of congress took place, Mr. Speaker, we heard the President of the United States make his address to the nation and I was most impressed, as I am sure you were, Mr. Speaker, with the opening of congress that day. Naturally security guards were all over the place. The galleries were packed, and when everything was ready Speaker Rayburn and Vice-President Nixon came to the platform. Then the usher-at-large announced that the ambassadors from foreign countries were entering the house, and they formed a wonderful group for us to see. Then the judges of the supreme court, in their full flowing gowns, walked down the aisle to their seats at the front. Then the members of the cabinet were introduced and walked down the aisle in a body. Then, as is the usual custom-no doubt many of you have seen this on television or listened to the proceedings on radio-the Speaker appointed four or five senators to accompany the President of the United States into the chamber. The President, of course, received a great deal of applause when his entrance was announced.
In the afternoon we were taken to the United States Senate where they have, I believe, 92 members, and one thing struck me very forcibly. Senator Aiken, one of the finest and oldest senators, said to me, "The welcome will take about five minutes. I will simply introduce each of you individually, and then you will walk halfway down the floor of the Senate and stand there. The whole thing will soon be over." I want to say to hon. members that the reception accorded us in the Senate that afternoon, as many senators told us afterwards, was unprecedented in the history of that chamber. Instead of the welcome taking five minutes it took a full 40 minutes, and it certainly warmed the cockles of our hearts when one senator after another rose to his feet in order to welcome us. It made us feel very much at home.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and the permission of the house I should like to put on Hansard as an appendix the proceedings on that occasion as found in the Congressional Record. I am sure the speeches of

The Address-Mr. Houck
welcome by the senators will be of interest to all members of the house. I should like to have permission, Mr. Speaker, to put this on the record.

speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, the
Speaker of the other place expressed the purpose of our meetings very well when he said:
This committee will fill a gap in the exchanges of thought between our two countries. We now have exchanges on the diplomatic level and the cabinet level, both confidential, but these exchanges between the rank and file of our legislatures will be less secret and meet an apparent need.
We as members of this committee look forward to important mutual benefits to Canada and the United States from the possibilities of future understanding and cooperation. A short time ago two reports were presented to the eighty-fifth congress, second session, House of Representatives, by Hon. Brooks Hays of Arkansas and Hon. Frank Coffin of Maine. I want to refer to what they said in summing up the situation. I was greatly impressed when I read their report. The thing that impressed me most was that after ten months of investigation on their part into our trade relations with the United States and the influence of the republic to the south on our overseas markets, we were really going to get some place. It was refreshing indeed to see a United States congressional committee arrive at some very definite conclusions, conclusions that virtually agreed with those of our statesmen.
I am sure these conclusions summarize the opinions of the predominant majority of Canadian businessmen. Their report recommended that Americans investing in Canada ought to be doubly responsive to Canadian sensitivity and employ as many Canadians as possible. The report adds that Canadians fear that Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies will be shut down if depression hits the United States, and that the Canadian market will again be saturated with United States products. It also urges that no upward changes in United States tariffs should be made without exploring all other possibilities, that revisions of tariffs should always be subject to review, and that businessmen should not be involved in too much red
tape at the border. It recognizes as well that the great Canadian aluminium plants were developed to supply the United States market and that Canadians do not therefore appreciate the United States imposing a duty on a product that is being produced here at their request. The report is also critical of the recent report of the United States tariff commission proposing increased duties on lead and zinc which might throw whole Canadian towns on the unemployment lists. They also recommended, and I think rightly so, that the United States consider the interests of Canada as an exporter before dumping goods on foreign markets or selling them on terms that practically exclude Canadian competition.
One thought that struck me forcibly was that seldom since the beginning of the high tariff age has a United States congressional report been so unselfish in its proposals. Certainly if it is accepted by congress it will be of great benefit to Canada at the present time and will give our own businessmen more confidence in the future. I know that we as members of parliament, including those who were members of the committee that visited Washington, certainly hope that the old guard will not liquidate the report, and that it will meet with the approval of congress. There were, of course, more recommendations made but the fact remains that something is being done, and I think this is the important thing, to improve relations between the two countries.
During our recent visit to Washington one United States senator said to me, "We feel it is important to know what you Canadians really think about us." My obvious answer to that, of course, was, "We would like to know what you think of us." But I also added that we could get along famously if the United States did not take us for granted, which would be a very great mistake. It is most important, Mr. Speaker, that we in Canada do not take the United States for granted, and that the people of the United States do not take Canadians for granted. I could not help but feel as a result of this conference-I know this feeling will be stronger as time marches on-that although there are a lot of dark spots in this troubled world there are certainly a number of bright spots as well, and one of them is the genuine friendship Canadians and Americans have for each other and the deep respect each country has for the other. We need only to think how different it is in other parts of the world where troops guard frontiers, where suspicion and mistrust are rampant, and where the attempt to spread an undemocratic

The Address-Mr. Houck ideology has resulted in chaos and has handicapped the reconstruction of the world after the most disastrous war in history.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is some 140 years since the Rush-Bagot treaty was signed which brought peace between our countries. We have gotten along very well since then, although at times there have been sources of irritation. Even after this treaty was signed there were still two sources of irritation to be settled, one of which was cleaned up by the Webster-Ashburton treaty of 1842 which settled the boundary line between New Brunswick and Maine. Then there was a further arbitration in 1846 which decided the boundary line between Canada and Alaska. The story from that time on has been one of increasing co-operation between Canada and the United States.
I want to say this, Mr. Speaker. We say we do not have any forts along our boundary line between these two countries. As I said in Washington we have larger forts over here, and the thing of which I am proud, and I say this to hon. members of this house, is that these forts are strong structures that will stand for a lifetime because they are based on what we call friendship. We invite the people of the United States to come here. I might use that old, familiar saying in this connection: "Happy to meet, sorry to part, happy to meet again". Why should we not welcome these people? We have been partners in two of the greatest wars ever fought. Our soldiers have fallen side by side with those of the United States in the common defence of a way of life which we believe to be best.
These two wars, especially the last one, have been followed by the cementing of closer ties. As I said, I live on the border between our two great countries, so I am continually reminded of the fact that the unguarded border between the United States and Canada is indeed a magnificent symbol of the real meaning of friendship. One cannot help but feel that if the world wants a formula for peace it should turn to the northern hemisphere. Our two great countries, Canada and the United States, have proven to the other peoples of the world that two nations can live side by side, not in fear but indeed in friendship. Over the years we have demonstrated again and again, as we did in the conference just concluded and will continue to do in the future, the value of getting together on problems of mutual concern.
In my opinion the real significance of our relationship with the United States is the fact that in spite of differences we have had peace, and in spite of our difficulties we have,


indeed, had friendship. Surely it is a comparatively easy thing to get along when there is nothing to quarrel about. We have had disputes, and we are going to have future disputes. We will be able to settle them in a friendly way, though at times we will have to talk frankly to each other. Certainly these discussions will not threaten our friendship in any way whatever. So far as I am concerned the United States-Canadian border is the main street of North America. Our fellowship with one another finds its inspiration in our mutual respect for freedom and our joint belief in the dignity and worth of the individual human being. It is further buttressed by our determination to safeguard the welfare and security of our people, and our resolve to maintain and defend the essential values of our society.
I have always felt that Canadians are like the people of the United States in their strong determination never to be found on the backs of the weak or at the feet of the strong, but we will be at the side of those who believe in freedom and democracy as we do. I think our history is now at the crossroads. Our deliberations in parliament, and the policies we follow, will affect future generations to come. I feel we must never lose sight of the fact when we are defining these policies that the great question of our time is whether the world will follow the high road to freedom or stumble into the dead-end street of communism. This government, as well as we in the opposition, has two or three aims. First, we must safeguard our freedom; we must maintain economic stability, and we must care for the human problems of individual citizens. In my opinion the greatest threat to democracy and freedom comes from within ourselves. We as members of parliament must have the courage to lead and to discharge our responsibilities in an effective and fearless way. Democracy, freedom and responsibility go hand in hand. If we lose one we lose all.
I always take a lot of pride, Mr. Speaker, in talking about the rainbow arch at Niagara Falls, which is visible most of the time during the day. It always seems to me that is a symbol of peace and friendship between two great countries.
They told us in Washington that history was made as a result of the formation of this interparliamentary committee. Senator Aiken said he did not know of any other countries the two legislative bodies of which had met at the same level. I should like to refer to what the correspondent of the Financial Post in Washington said. He said that a major improvement in Canada-U.S. economic relations may have occurred with the agreement on a Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group.

I think the Speaker of our house said, and it was very apropos, that this fills a gap in the relations between the two countries, and we hope these discussions will be as broad as possible.
Then again, the Financial Post said that it is from congress that most of Canada's miseries with Uncle Sam stem, and hence a better congressional awareness of Canada can be a highly beneficial result of these parliamentary-congressional meetings. When Senator Aiken, the senator to whom I referred a few minutes ago, said good-bye to us he said that never before in its history had the United States congress established such close legislative links with another country. I say, therefore, that this interparliamentary group has made history, and as one newspaper so rightly said it will give us a direct channel into the United States congress.
I should like to plead with this government, Mr. Speaker, to do something about paying at least 50 per cent of the expenses of the Belleville McFarland's hockey team which will carry Canada's colours into the world hockey tournament in the coming months. As I understand it this club is looking for $50,000. I think it is a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada that this club has to ask councils in various cities and towns of the province, as well as various citizens, to share in the expenses of this team. I understand the larger cities have been asked for one-tenth of one cent per person. This does not amount to much, but it certainly seems to me that when we consider the honour this team will bring to Canada, the province from which the team comes and the federal government should each share 50 per cent of the cost. I do not feel the cost is excessive, because hockey seems to be our national game and we should at least be financially responsible for the expenses of this team. Many of these boys have good jobs, many of them have families to support, and certainly it is no encouragement to the boys on this hockey team to have to go begging for their expenses before they attempt to bring this signal honour to Canada. I hope that the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurer will see fit to make contributions toward the expenses of this team, and I know every member will wish them good luck, feeling that they will bring us a lot of credit and honour.
There is just one more thing I wish to mention, Mr. Speaker, and then I shall be finished. I should like to speak on something that is close to my heart in my own riding of Niagara Falls. This matter affects not only silverware companies in Niagara Falls but indeed silverware companies all over Canada. I must admit that it is rather rough
The Address-Mr. Houck going when these companies are up against the price competition of stainless steel from Japan.
In the first place, Japanese imports of flat silverware into Canada for the first six months of 1958 were 1,368,000 dozen. In the second place, that amount is three times as much as Japan has imported into Canada in any equivalent period. In the third place, Japanese exports to Canada in the month of June last exceeded exports to the United States for the first time in history, the actual figures being more than 300,000 dozen to Canada versus 260,000 dozen to the United States.
Japanese imports into Canada last year by volume were about double the output of all Canadian manufacturers combined. It seems obvious that the Japanese are dumping into Canada the production that the United States quota prevents them from shipping to that country. Certainly the final result of this situation will be that unless we make some quota arrangements in the near future, we shall have no stainless steel industry here in Canada. The only conclusion one can draw is that once this industry is forced to close down because it cannot meet Japanese competition, it is doubtful if it will ever start again. The decline in Japanese exports to the United States was more than offset by the increased export shipments to Canada which took place during the first six months of 1958. In June, 1958, Canada's purchases of stainless steel tableware from Japan topped purchases made by the United States.
In Niagara Falls we have three large silverware companies. Because of the importation of this flat silverware from Japan, employment in at least two of these companies has been decreased by over 50 per cent as compared with what it was twelve months ago. I certainly hope the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance will take steps to correct this situation as soon as possible. It is an alarming situation as far as we are concerned. If this condition could be rectified it would be of material assistance with regard to the unemployment situation in the Niagara district.
May I say this in closing, Mr. Speaker, and I say it with all the sincerity possible. I hope the members of this house will take a great interest in this committee which was formed some time ago and about which I spoke. When hon. members are asked to serve on this committee I hope they will find the time to do so. They will find it well worth while to meet these gentlemen from the United States.
I want to say this, and I do so because of experience. When you are talking to these

The Address-Mr. Harkness senators and members of the House of Representatives, you are in the world series, you are talking in big time, and you must be on your mettle. They have the same feeling that we have. It is the uppermost feeling in our hearts and minds that we want to do everything we can for Canada. They want to do everything they can for the United States. We want to stand on our own feet. We are out to protect the rights of Canada. They are out to protect the rights of the United States. But when the final conclusion is arrived at, it will be a definite conclusion to the benefit of the great republic of the United States and of our great Dominion of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations to those already proffered by so many members of the house to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is a particular pleasure for me to congratulate these gentlemen. The mover made an excellent speech on agriculture, a subject on which he is particularly well qualified to speak. The seconder made one of the finest maiden speeches which has ever been heard in this house.
I am going to devote my remarks today entirely to agriculture. I have, of course, practically nothing to deal with in the way of criticism as far as the Leader of the Opposition is concerned. In his speech of two hours and twenty minutes, or 140 minutes, he devoted nearly half a minute to agriculture. This was rather summary treatment, Mr. Speaker, for the industry on which more of our people are still dependent, either directly or indirectly, than on any other industry in Canada. However, when the Leader of the Opposition was engaging in such great flights of fancy and imagination probably we should not expect him to devote his thoughts and his time to anything so down to earth as our food supply and the farmers who produce it. The closest the Leader of the Opposition managed to get to agriculture, practically, was the setting up of straw men and then knocking them down.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, what did he say in this nearly one-half minute which he devoted to agriculture? It consisted chiefly of a gibe at the Prime Minister and myself, and a statement that confusion existed with regard to agriculture. I think in the next few minutes I can demonstrate that there is not and never has been any confusion as far as we are concerned in our agricultural policies. This attempt on the part of the Leader of the Opposition, which was followed up by one of his supporters, to demonstrate or make

out that there is a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and myself with regard to agriculture is completely without foundation.
On numerous occasions the Prime Minister has spoken on the desirability of a world food bank and of a NATO food bank, and by this means making use of the large agricultural production which we have in Canada. I think everybody in this chamber and everybody concerned with agriculture throughout the country is aware of the desirability of those ideas coming to fruition. However, at the present time neither of those schemes is in actual operation. turkeys and fowl. We placed all forms of butter and butter fat under price support and import control; we set up a royal commission on price spreads which is still sitting and which has made a very exhaustive investigation of price spreads, and the effect of its activities and its report will, I think, be very beneficial not only to farmers but also to consumers.

I congratulate him on his being elected member for the constituency of Springfield. I might also tell him that if he got in with a lower majority in the by-election, he need not ascribe this to loss of personal popularity but rather to the unpopularity of the government now in charge of the destinies of this country. I wish him a rewarding stay in our national parliament, albeit a short one, as you will readily appreciate, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to refer to only one remark made by the hon. member for Springfield, the one about the young Liberals of Canada. Yesterday evening, the hon. member for Springfield said that Canada's young Liberals do not have, within their own party, the same freedom of expression which the young Conservatives enjoy. Well, Mr. Speaker, I must tell the hon. member that I have had the privilege and honour of being president of the Young Liberals Association of Canada, and that at no time were its members hampered in their work. On the contrary, Liberal party officials always sought out the advice of the young Liberals, and such suggestions as might contribute to the welfare of our fellow citizens. They always took keen interest in proposals put forward by the young Liberals, and young Liberals have at all times enjoyed full and complete freedom within the party. I do not know how it is with young Conservatives in Canada, and my interest in the matter is only lukewarm, I confess.
I should also like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Jorgenson and Fortin).
The hon. member for Provencher, honoured by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) by being entrusted with the task of proposing the address, did so in concrete, concise and intelligent fashion. I congratulate him. He told us about an area of Canada which is of interest to all of us in western Canada.
I should like also to offer special congratulations to the new member for Montmagny-L'lslet. I had the opportunity of meeting him during the last campaign and, needless to say, it was in the constituency of Montmagny-L'lslet, where I had gone to help in the election not of him but of someone else. I congratulate him in particular on his election, and say to him that he is assuming a very great responsibility, because he now has a rich heritage to develop, the heritage of 25 years of Liberal representation in the constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet. He is the successor to a man who honoured the province, a man who did much for Canadian politics, the Hon. Jean Lesage.
If the Hon. Jean Lesage has left the federal scene, it was not of his own choice. He did it out of a sense of duty, to help fight the dictatorship which is plaguing the province of Quebec, and the work he is now doing in the province is for the defence of democracy. I am sure that this task he has undertaken, with all the sacrifices it involves, will bear fruit and that the man who will crush dictatorship in the province of Quebec and who will become the province's next prime minister will be the former representative of the constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet in the House of Commons, Hon. Mr. Speaker, I was deeply impressed by the speech made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, particularly when he touched upon national unity. One of the main reasons that led me to enter politics was my desire to contribute to the building up of national unity in this great and beautiful country. I was most particularly impressed when the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet stated in his speech:
I honestly and truly believe these views to be genuinely representative of the province of Quebec.
He said that the province of Quebec was "a province like any other province". Indeed it is true, Mr. Speaker, that the great majority of Canadian citizens in the province of Quebec believe their province is like other provinces.
A few years ago, when that great statesman, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, was prime minister of this country and represented a constituency that is located in the very heart of the province of Quebec, he stated in a memorable speech that he too was of the opinion that the majority of citizens in the province of Quebec believed their province like any other province.
Who, at that time, rose to say that the province of Quebec was not a province like the others? It was the premier of the province of Quebec. He protested the words of Mr. St. Laurent, branding Mr. St. Laurent a traitor to his province.
And who, following the lead of the premier of Quebec, rose to say that the province of Quebec was not a province like other

The Address-Mr. Rouleau provinces? Ministers, Union Nationale members of the legislature, and Union Nationale party hacks.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet and to assure him of my unreserved admiration for having the courage to assert in this house, that the province of Quebec is a province like any other province.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker. As usual I shall comply with your directions and will discuss problems that concern the central and provincial governments, as in the case of grants to universities.
When my hon. friend interrupted, I was commenting on grants to universities. There is another matter in the same field, Mr. Speaker, that I want to mention. If the province of Quebec is like all the other provinces why does its premier systematically refuse to join the hospital-insurance plan initiated by the former Liberal government and implemented by the present government?
If the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), is sincere, and means what he said in this house, I ask him to use such influence as he may have on the provincial government to say to the leader of the government of the province of Quebec, that since Quebec is a province like all other provinces, it should participate in the Canadian way of life, and in all truly Canadian projects. Moreover, the best emissary he could send to the premier of the province of Quebec-in case he has no direct access to him-would be the Hon. Antoine Rivard, a member of the Duplessis cabinet, who campaigned very actively in favour of the new member for Montmagny-L'Islet and who, in fact, is largely responsible for his victory.
The great majority of Canadians, Mr. Speaker, of whatever racial origin, in whatever province they were born, have realized they are part of a large family, the great Canadian family. I am glad that Canadians from sea to sea, have finally realized that they belong to Canada first. As a young Canadian from

the province of Quebec, who has had the opportunity to travel across the country, I do say that, personally, I feel just as much at home in Vancouver, in Winnipeg, in Saskatoon, in Toronto or anywhere else in Canada, as I do in my province.
It is for this reason that I wanted to offer very special congratulations to the new member for Montmagny-L'Islet.
He made very appropriate remarks on national unity, although he could perhaps have gone a bit further, particularly in the light of recent statements by two members of the present cabinet. In fact, quite recently in a speech which she made in Toronto the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) stated, in the face of all of Canada, that the national anthem O Canada was perhaps a pretty song, but was not the Canadian national anthem.
I sincerely regret that, while speaking of national unity, the member for Montmagny-L'lslet did not see fit to point out those falsehoods. As was said by the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier), even if the national anthem O Canada is not set down as the national anthem of this country, since Canadian parliamentary institutions all came down to us from British parliamentary institutions, where tradition prevails, and since O Canada has been sung and accepted for years and years, I say that the only national anthem we have is O Canada.
Besides, along similar lines, Mr. Speaker, I really regret that, after dealing with national unity, the honourable member for Montmagny-L'Islet did not see fit to suggest the adoption of a distinctively Canadian flag, one that all Canadians could be rightly proud of, whatever their country of origin, whatever the province they live in, and which would be a symbol through which they would honour their country.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to this house and to the country that I am in favour of a Canadian flag having no sign emblematic of other areas than our own. I want an essentially Canadian flag, devoid of any mark which might suggest to other countries that this is not a free country.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet deserves the congratulations of all the members and of all Canadians for speaking the way he did on national unity. But we cannot say as much about the other issues he covered.

unemployment.

Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) stated a few days ago, before a meeting of young Conservatives in Quebec city, that unemployment in Canada should be considered as an heritage left by the previous government. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said a few days ago, as reported in the Gazette, that everything was fine in the country and that we were heading again for a golden era. That is not what I would call facing up to one's responsibilities to ensure a bright future for our country.

If in a country as rich as this, a man with a family is unable to earn a living, how can the people have confidence in this government? While Canadians can rightly feel confident of their country's future, it is also true that they have grounds to feel pessimistic with respect to the leadership given to the country by this short-sighted government on whose shoulders rests the responsibility for unemployment, for the recession and for inflation. The members on the government side apparently have not yet recovered from their honeymoon. They never expected to gain power in 1957, and they travelled across the country making irresponsible promises.
Mr. Speaker, my attention is drawn to the fact that there is at the moment no minister in the house. This shows the extent of their interest in the affairs of the nation, and it also shows, as I have just stated to the house, that the members of the cabinet are still on their honeymoon.
As I was saying, the members of the cabinet and members of the government stalked the country in 1957, promising heaven on earth.

Mr. Speaker, may I first join with several hon. members who have preceded me and who have expressed their approval of and their satisfaction in the fact that you will again preside over the deliberations in this house. During the period that I have had the honour to represent Queens-Lunenburg I could not help but be impressed by your ability, your fairness and your sense of duty and I am certain that the affairs of this house will be conducted during this session as in the past in fairness to all and with approval of the whole house.
I would like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the mover, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson), and the seconder, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Though separated by great distances these two hon. gentlemen have two things in common. They have youth and an earnest desire to assist the people who have elected them to this parliament.
As one of the members from Nova Scotia I should like, on behalf of the people of that province and of the people of my own constituency of Queens-Lunenburg, to have the opportunity to voice our appreciation of the outstanding work done by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in the past year. He has at all times lent a very sympathetic ear to our problems and the people of my constituency are pleased with the work that has been done and the work that has been planned for the coming year. Many of those projects are long overdue. In addition to providing much needed facilities for the people in the riding they are also providing work. In complimenting the minister may I say I hope he will not become complacent because there is still a number of projects awaiting his attention in the constituency, and if I should be insistent and impatient I hope he will realize that I am only trying to better the condition of the people I represent.
In complimenting the minister I would also like to make reference to the simultaneous translation system which has been installed in this chamber in a building which comes under the supervision of the Department of Public Works. I am sure all of us appreciate the provision of this new facility; it has improved our enjoyment of the debates and

I would like to suggest to the government that this facility be extended to the galleries so that those of the public who are interested in the affairs of parliament and in the government of this country may also enjoy the debates as they are carried on in both languages.
I should like at this time, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of Queens-Lunenburg to renew our pledges of loyalty to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). My words are most inadequate to express to him our feelings for what he has done for my constituency, for Nova Scotia and for Canadians generally. His recent tour did much to strengthen the ties of friendship among the countries which he visited and in travelling throughout my riding I found that there could be no mistaking the great depth of feeling and admiration in which he is held by everyone.
I have the honour to represent the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg in Nova Scotia. It is a constituency that is bound on the east by the dual riding of Halifax and Colchester-Hants, on the north by the riding represented by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), Dibgy-Annapolis-Kings, on the west by Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare and on the south by that mighty, moody, restless taskmaster, the Atlantic ocean.
My people in Queens county are primarily engaged in lumbering, farming, fishing and industry. They have one of the largest pulp and paper mills in Canada, located in Brooklyn, and certainly one of the most efficient. In Lunenburg county my people are engaged in farming with some lumbering and manufacturing industries, as well as both inshore and deepsea fishing operations. In this county my home town was founded in 1753 by thrifty, God-fearing Hanoverians, French and Swiss colonists. Lunenburg preserves today a quality and an atmosphere unique among towns in the maritimes. There is a quality of individualism about those people which extends throughout the length and breadth of my constituency.
When Queens-Lunenburg was settled there were the usual hardships which the colonists endured; occasional and bloodthirsty attacks were made on outlying farms by Micmac and Malecite Indians, and during the American revolutionary war the coastal towns of Liverpool and Lunenburg were frequently raided by ships from Salem and other east coast ports. In spite of those handicaps, however, our people progressed and the heritage of the original settlers has been cherished from generation to generation. Because of our geographic location our economy throughout the years has revolved around ships and the sea.

The Address-Mr. Crouse
In its wake the fishing industry has brought to my constituency a whole fleet of allied industries, all of which are in a healthy and expanding condition: marine engine manufacturers in Chester, Lunenburg, Bridgewater and Liverpool and builders of wooden ships of all sizes in Chester, Mahone Bay, Lunenburg, Dayspring and the Liverpool area. In addition to this, Liverpool and Lunenburg can boast of marine railways for the hauling of ships as well as adequate refitting yards to carry out necessary repairs, and during the past war those yards contributed to the war effort by suitably refitting naval vessels, minesweepers, corvettes and frigates.
I mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, because here is a constituency that has literally pulled itself up by its own bootstraps. Forced from the beginning to make their living from the soil or from the sea, there is no more rugged group of individuals in Canada than the good people of my riding. By their own efforts and with very little help they have maintained a fairly high level of employment throughout the years. This was accomplished by careful planning, saving, perseverance, diligence and hard work, and the same is true today.
We have heard since the beginning of this session about the unemployment problem that affects some parts of Canada and the insistent effort by members of the opposition to lay the unemployment problem at the feet of the government. We are all aware of the unemployment situation existing throughout Canada today and every responsible member of the house is kept constantly informed of conditions within his own riding. Unemployment is not something new. Recessions and unemployment go hand in hand, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) left no doubt about the inheritance of the government when he used these words on Monday, January 19, as found at page 35 of Hansard, as he looked across at the government benches, "those men who later could not see it when they were in the middle of it."
Yes, Mr. Speaker, in 1957 we were in the middle of our inherited recession. We took over a leaky ship of state and we immediately set to work to make our ship seaworthy. We are now on course and we are sailing steadily forward despite efforts by members of the opposition to rock the boat. Unemployment is not something that just happens by itself and it will not be cured by the foghorn-like bellowing we have experienced in the last few days from hon. members of the opposition and the C.C.F. The government has instituted a most effective program of winter work to cope with this situation but the two opposition parties have as many 66968-9-18J
criticisms of this program to relieve unemployment as there are dogfish on a summer trawl line and they are about as valuable.
Increased social and welfare benefits, as suggested by both opposition parties, are not the answer at the present time. Such programs only redistribute money. They do not create wealth. For the most part the people in my riding, who make their living from the sea and the soil and from lumbering, know that you can only share that which is first earned and the greater the earnings the greater the share for each person. They long ago learned that the only way their standard of living could be improved was by increasing production and sales, and their present standards were achieved by hard work and dedication to their tasks.
I believe the time has come for Canadians to stop and consider the foundations upon which this country's progress and the people's high living standards and the social security they now enjoy really rest. It was not socialism that built Canada's great cities, towns and villages. It was not state planning that directed the pioneers to explore and open up this great country or provide Canada with the manufacturing industries that give employment to many thousands of people. It was not government that brought the country's great resource industries into being. It was not officialdom that created an economy prosperous enough to provide such things as unemployment insurance, old age pensions and family allowances. No, Mr. Speaker, Canada's growth, prosperity and high living standards were built in a different way.
They developed because people were able to save with confidence, to invest freely, to take risks in new enterprises and to expect a reasonable reward for their initiative. These were the foundations upon which confederation was established and, while some of them lost money, while others were rewarded for their risk-taking, the greatest beneficiaries were the people of Canada themselves. They were provided with the goods and services they needed or wanted at prices that they were willing or able to pay. These prices were determined freely by bargaining between buyers and sellers in the open market place. I believe these basic truths are worth remembering today because the growth of Canada and the prosperity of Canadians in the future, certainly no less than in the past, depend upon such factors as incentive, savings and investment.
There is a dangerous trend evident in the thinking of many Canadians. This trend is fostered and abetted by socialist groups in Canada, not all of whom travel under the

The Address-Mr. Crouse label of the eight members in the far corner of this chamber. These socialists abhor the word "profit" ignoring the fact that when we do not have profits business and industry close down and we see loss of employment. Without profits less funds are available for expansion of existing industries and for the opening up of new industries. These are the two big sources for new jobs. Without profits less funds are available for the purchase of better tools, and in today's business world modernization is the key to success. The firm that cannot buy new tools cannot compete with those who do and goes out of business. Without profits there are no funds for new research or new product development and growth and expansion are stopped.
The plain truth is that profits create more jobs while losses create unemployment. If we are to move out of the present unemployment situation we must provide a healthy economic atmosphere in Canada for the free growth and expansion of our large and small business enterprises.
My home town of Lunenburg this year celebrates 206 years of free enterprise and progress. There is a business firm there named Zwicker and Company which has been active for 170 of those 206 years and their belief is that such a record would not have been possible under socialism, communism or any of the other isms except, of course, capitalism. This is the point I wish to prove and the belief to which I subscribe. In a growing nation with an expanding economy I believe that capitalism and free enterprise, if given an opportunity, can and will provide the answer to all our employment problems.
As I come from a maritime riding I should like to say a few words about shipbuilding, ship repairing, their allied industries and their importance to Canada. I am pleased to note in the speech from the throne that an amendment will be presented to the Canada Shipping Act. Canadian shipyards are widely separated geographically. To take care of the needs of international sea transport and the coasting trade, shipyards are required in the maritimes, the St. Lawrence area, on the great lakes and the Pacific coast of Canada. In fact, fully integrated organizations of design and technical forces and skilled shipyard personnel and facilities must be maintained in four separate and distinct areas for commercial purposes as well as for reasons of national security.
Shipyards and navies go together. The Royal Canadian Navy cannot function without shipyards in Canada to service and repair its ships and to build new ones as required. It must also have the assurance that shipyards will be available and ready to repair major

damages that its ships may suffer in the event of war. In addition, facilities must be available for servicing Canada's inland and coastal fleets, the government's own service vessels and foreign vessels calling at Canadian ports.
The level of employment in the shipbuilding industry is steadily dropping and unless positive steps are taken it will continue to decline. At the peak of the naval building program more than 15,500 men were working in the shipyards. In October of this year employment had dropped to slightly over 10,000, the lowest figure since 1950 when the naval rebuilding program was first started. Of the fourteen destroyer escort vessels in that program, nine have been commissioned and are in service with the Royal Canadian Navy. The remaining ships will be completed and commissioned some time this year. This shipbuilding program enabled shipyards in the four strategic areas of Canada to build up competent teams of skilled workers. The completed ships have undergone tests and their performance has exceeded the expectations of their designers and builders.
They have drawn praise from our friends and allies the British, Swedes and Norwegians. The shipyard teams, with their special skills to build these fine ships, are now being rapidly disbanded as a result of the slowdown in naval shipbuilding. It is true that this condition has been alleviated to some extent by shipbuilding orders placed by the Department of Transport. While this work has been helpful, it is not sufficient to keep a reasonable proportion of our yards busy.
Our Canadian way of life, with its high wage structures, results in Canadian shipbuilding prices being considerably higher than those applying in Japan, Germany, Great Britain and other competitive shipbuilding nations. Since Canadian shipyards cannot match competitive costs, orders for export shipbuilding are out of the question. Few orders can be expected from Canadian ocean ship operators who feel they cannot add to the relatively high operating costs the first cost of building their ships in Canada unless some special incentive is offered to offset the high first cost. The only remaining potential source of commercial orders is the building and repairing of ships for the Canadian coasting trade and the fishing industry.
In the event that the recommendations to the royal commission on the coasting trade are looked upon with favour by the government, this source of business will disappear entirely. Despite the predictions that Canadian flag shipping in the coasting trade will end when the useful life of the existing fleet is terminated and its place taken by

ships built and registered in the United Kingdom, the royal commission took the view that the marine industry in Canada should be dispensed with rather than helped. The fate of the Canadian shipbuilding industry, according to the royal commission, is to become little more than a repair industry. This, Mr. Speaker, is dangerous thinking. Most trading nations of the world have recognized the need to foster the development of their shipping and shipbuilding industries, and they have adopted policies of one form or another to encourage their maintenance.
The United States has the most liberal policy of all nations for aiding its marine industries, and I am not thinking of "Liberal" in the sense that the opposition may be thinking of it. From as far back as 1817 United States coastwise trade has been reserved by statute to vessels built in the United States and owned and operated by United States citizens. This assistance takes the form of cargo preference provisions, tax benefits, mortgage aid and trade-in allowances. All of these things have served to keep a large tonnage of United States merchant ships on ocean trade which otherwise would have disappeared. A study of other major shipping nations, including the United Kingdom, will show that they have found it necessary to grant some form of assistance, financial or otherwise, to maintain their fleets and to compete in the highly competitive field of international shipping.
I do not suggest that this government propose a program of aid as extensive as that being carried out by the people of the United States. However, I do believe we should have a well defined national policy of aids, similar to those adopted by other large shipping and exporting nations, which would create the proper economic climate in which our shipyards could secure orders. I believe a shipbuilding and ship-repairing industry in Canada, with adequate continuing production, is an indispensable need in a troubled world. Canada and Canadians cannot afford to allow their shipyards to become progressively less busy until they disappear. Without some measure of aid the Canadian shipbuilding industry will gradually disappear and Canada will have lost an essential instrument of defence.
Speaking of defence, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of another important point which I would like to bring to the attention of this government. The speech from the throne makes reference to NATO in these words:
In concert with its allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Canada has reaffirmed its determination to maintain and improve the power of the alliance as a deterrent against aggression.
The Address-Mr. Crouse
We are all aware today of the great expense involved in maintaining the early warning radar bases in the northern parts of Canada and of the great emphasis placed upon the government's decision regarding the CF-105 and its alternative the American-made Bomarc missile. I do not wish to minimize the importance of these decisions, but wish to point out that all of them are based on the theory that Canada and the United States only need defence on a north and south basis. What about our east and our west coasts. Canada is touched by the sea on both the east and west coasts. The great oceans of the world are essential to the economic well-being of our country in that they produce a yearly harvest of fish and carry our commerce to the four corners of the world. They are, therefore, vital to our continued existence as a free and civilized nation.
These same great oceans, however, also shelter within their depths the greatest threat to the security of this country that we have ever been called upon to face. This menace is the submarine, a sinister black shape, lethal, invisible, and stalking its prey from under the sea. Today, the Russian undersea fleet numbers between 500 and 600 submarines. This total is increasing steadily under the impetus of a huge naval building program. While some of these submarines may be obsolete it is known that following the armistice the Russians acquired several of the most advanced types of German U-boats developed in the late stages of the war.
The harnessing of atomic power has seen its first application to ship propulsion in the submarine, and has immediately resulted in higher speeds, especially when submerged, and in the capability of remaining under the surface for almost indefinite periods. The submarine was always a formidable weapon of war, and it would now appear to have acquired a measure of superiority over its enemies which makes it extremely difficult to combat. In addition, when you add to its already greatly increased efficiency the capability of launching ballistic and guided missiles, not only from the surface but from submerged positions as well, the submarine becomes a most dangerous foe.
Let us analyse this threat to Canada. We have heard discussions of this subject. We have heard questions asked about where ballistic missile bases would be placed in Canada. We place a great deal of importance on this problem. The modern submarine can be employed as a commerce raider attacking merchant ships singly or in convoy, as a minelayer or as a missile launching platform. As a minelayer it is quite capable of entering

The Address-Mr. Crouse a port, laying mines and leaving the area without anyone knowing that it has done its work. It is as a guided missile launcher that the submarine poses its greatest threat. From a position off either of Canada's three great coastlines, the Atlantic, Pacific or Arctic, which are approximately 60,000 miles long, a missile-equipped submarine could send its death-dealing projectile far into the heart of this country. Whole cities, huge industrial areas, and many of our most important defence installations lie within range of these invisible foes. One missile, fitted with a nuclear warhead, is enough to destroy any one of these areas.
Any aggressor nation planning an atomic war could not find a more suitable weapon than the modern missile-firing submarine. Under international law and because of its own invisibility such a submarine can roam the oceans of the world at will. It can carry out surveys-believe me they are carrying out surveys, for I am in the fishing industry and receive reports from my captains that these submarines of unknown origin are operating on the Atlantic ocean, some of them fairly close to the fishing banks that lie off the east coast. As I said, it can carry out surveys and compile the charts that are necessary to determine the exact position from which to launch an attack, so the danger and the threat are obvious. It is an extremely difficult and tremendous task, requiring large numbers of men and materials, to counter this threat.
However, it must be done; and with the full support of the people of Canada and our allies of other NATO nations, it can be done. The prize in any future war will not be Europe with its overcrowded cities, but Canada with its unlimited resources and its room to expand. Here then is a challenge to the people of this country and to the government to take immediate steps to increase our own submarine fleet. In this way we could demonstrate that any attack against us would be doomed to failure and also that we possess the means, if necessary, to counterattack.
Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to say a few words about our fishing industry. During the past year there has been a marked shortage of groundfish on the Atlantic coast. When I spoke of groundfish, my seatmate asked if that was something similar to hamburger. I should therefore like to explain, to those who are not familiar with this term, that groundfish is not hamburger made out of fish. The term applies to those fish which are caught in prolific quantities off the east coast and which consist mainly of cod, haddock, pollock, hake, cusk, and rosefish, to name some of the leading
[Mr. Crouse.J

varieties. As I say, during the past year there has been a marked shortage of groundfish on the Atlantic coast, with exceptional declines shown in the landings of cod and haddock, with catches of both species being down 18 per cent and 23 per cent respectively as compared with last year. This shortage has resulted in a staple market for fresh and frozen fish and has improved the prices paid to the primary producer. In fact, there has never before been a time in Canada's history when prices paid to the primary producer, the fisherman, were as high as they are today under the Conservative government.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) is present with us this afternoon for he is also to be complimented on the implementation of the new fresh fish inspection program which will become effective in April. This program will mean greater control over the quality of fish packaged by the many shore processing plants throughout the maritimes, and will enable fishermen who land a high quality product properly cleaned and iced to receive a better price for their catch, as the emphasis is now on quality. This emphasis has made the fisherman realize he is handling a food product, and this year, for the first time in Canada's history, fresh and frozen fish will be labelled "government inspected'' or "Processed under government supervision". The implementation of this program should provide a boost for fishery products generally, for the Canadian housewife will be able to buy fish so labelled, with every confidence that she is getting the finest product available.
In the salt fish industry, however, there is a different story, with some troublesome marketing problems. Our salt fish exporters have had a favourable market in the Dominican Republic. However, this republic has a very unfavourable trade balance with Canada, and we know what that means. We have heard a good bit of comment about unfavourable trade balances. In 1957 they imported from Canada goods to the value of $5 million, and their exports to Canada had a value of only $1.3 million. The prosperity of the Dominican Republic depends upon agriculture, with sugar being their chief crop. Canada has not imported any raw sugar from the Dominican Republic since 1955, and the amount imported at that time was only 12,850 tons. The reason for this situation is that Canada extends a tariff preference on the raw sugar imports from commonwealth countries of $1 per 100 pounds, which tariff discriminates against non-commonwealth sugar producing countries such as the Dominican Republic. The inequity of this situation

is that Great Britain extends a lower preference on commonwealth raw sugar than does Canada, and Britain now imports the bulk of its sugar from the Dominican Republic.
On the other hand, Canadian fish exports to the Dominican Republic amount to about $1.5 million a year, and practically all of this fish consists of dried salt pollock, hake and bloaters. In fact, it is the most important single market for these products, taking over 50 per cent of the annual output of Nova Scotia's fishermen. It can readily be seen that this market constitutes an important source of income for a great number of our fishermen, particularly in western Nova Scotia.
Recently a Norwegian trade mission was in the Dominican Republic with a view to fostering greater trade between Norway and the republic. Should the republic take steps to divert its purchases of these fishery products to Norway, Mr. Speaker, you can well imagine the impact this action could have on this particular segment of our Nova Scotia fishing industry. Frankly, I know of no alternative market because, apart from British Guiana, salted pollock and hake are not preferred over salted cod in the Caribbean countries. Quite apart from the fact that sales to British Guiana could not be increased to a point of absorbing the surplus which would result through the loss of the Dominican Republic market, the republic invariably pays higher prices for these products.
In view of the importance of this matter, I would request that the government review Canada's tariff preferences on raw sugar with a view to lessening the present discrimination against sugar imports from these noncommonwealth countries which are the most important salt fish markets for our maritime exporters. For the information of the house, I should like to point out that we sell more salt fish to non-commonwealth countries than we sell to commonwealth countries, and that existing tariff preferences to these commonwealth countries in the Caribbean are detrimental to our fishermen and work a hardship on the industry.
In the fresh fish industry the government's present assistance policy of $160 per gross ton on ships up to 65 feet in length has been of material help to many fishermen who operate small boats. However, experience has proved that on a year-round basis these small draggers cannot be operated economically. They are handicapped from December through to the following March by high winds and winter weather and consequently cannot operate, while they are faced with fixed charges such as radar rentals, radio telephone rentals
The Address-Mr. Crouse and insurance which constantly add to their expense and decrease their earnings.
I believe the time has arrived to encourage the building of larger boats which can fish twelve months of the year and can utilize the resources of our great offshore banks. Canada today is lagging behind some other countries in modernizing her fishing fleet, particularly trawlers; and any changes made in government policy should be with a view to assisting and encouraging the fishing industry to acquire the most modern implements of production. In my opinion, this step is absolutely necessary if our Canadian industry is to compete successfully in the catching of fish and to keep pace with these other producing countries. I believe this step is necessary if we are properly to expand and develop markets on this continent in the most economical way and if we are to operate efficiently and maintain full employment in the industry. I believe this step is also necessary if our processing plants are to have an adequate year-round supply of quality fish. To this end more encouragement should be given to the building up of a modern fleet of large trawlers which are the only productive units capable of keeping an adequate supply of fish on the market every month of the year.
With these objectives in mind I respectfully suggest that the government give consideration to the building of a modern fleet by instituting a system of investment allowances as is now being done in the United Kingdom. These increased depreciation allowances should run as high as 65 per cent and should apply on all ships built in Canadian yards. To guarantee the expansion of the fleet, the amount accumulated by these allowances should be made to apply toward the construction of new fishing draggers. In addition to this, I believe the present assistance plan offered by the government should be increased, as the cost of ship construction has advanced materially in recent years.
Of further and final interest to the fishermen of my riding is the present regulation which requires large Canadian trawlers to fish outside the 12 mile limit, while all trawlers, regardless of size, of any other nation are permitted to fish within three miles of our shores. I believe it is time this regulation was revoked, for it is a ridiculous situation which permits foreign trawlers to fish within three miles of our shores while it is illegal for some of our Canadian trawlers to fish within 12 miles of our coast. I realize that it is the desire of the Canadian government to bring about an international agreement on a 12 mile fishing limit, but charity begins at home, and until such time as this

The Address-Mr. Howard can be accomplished, this discrimination against our own larger trawlers should be removed. I firmly believe that implementation of these recommendations would be a great forward step for the Canadian Atlantic coast fishing industry and greatly improve working conditions for these hardy men who make their living on the sea.
