I should like first of all to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) who has just completed what I consider to be an excellent analysis of the problems of the fishermen on the Atlantic coast, and I hope that his representations with respect to year round fishing and with respect to the elimination of the foolish 12-mile and 3-mile limit business will eventually lead to action. I cannot, of course, extend any such remarks to him with respect to what the capitalist system can do and what it is good for; we all know that he and I disagree on that.
It appears to be a coincidence that today, as on the last occasion when I rose to take part in the debate on the address, the only cabinet minister present in the house should be the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). I hope that he and I are not going to develop this into a regular practice; the comments I may have to make about fishing will be reserved for another time when I am able to deal with this subject more specifically.
It is in no perfunctory way that I wish, in addition, to extend my congratulations to the hon. and attractive member for Gren-ville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) on her election to this house. It has always been my thought that there are far too few women who participate in politics; certainly far too few who have the privilege of being elected either to this house or to the provincial legislatures or to the municipal councils. I am sure that if we had more people in our public life possessing that peculiarly womanly trait of being able to get to the heart of a problem and then to suggest a solution, we would probably have much more sense arising out of the legislation we make. I say this in a general way, because, naturally, all members of the hon. lady's sex are not endowed with the same measure of ability. I wish


her well, and I hope that she along with her two colleagues, the other two lady members, will have some influence in the party caucus and bring some sense and logic to the decisions of this government, because certainly if there ever was a government which needed sense and logic brought to its attention, and influence imposed upon it, it is this one.
It is fitting that the opening of this session should take place in the month of January, because if I recall accurately what little knowledge I have of Roman mythology there was a Roman god called Janus after whom this month was named and this government, like Janus, has two faces, one of which it presents to the general public at election time, on television broadcasts and at social events. This is the face of help, the face of assistance, the face of promise. But it wears its other face when action is desired, whenever action is necessary as far as legislation is concerned.
Some of the backbenchers of the Conservative party who have taken part in this debate appear to have concentrated their attention on one small sentence in the speech from the throne. They appear to have been blinded by a mere 20 words in that speech and to have forgotten all the other matters which were omitted from it. The fascination and charm exercised by that one sentence have resulted in far too much buttering up of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)- far too many laudatory remarks about the government, references to individuals being the greatest Canadians who ever lived, and so on-the hope being that as a result some of them would be among those chosen few who would end up by being parliamentary secretaries.

Mr. Speaker, the manner in which this house over the years has developed its systems of conducting business would appear to require some changes. I intend to suggest some changes that should be made without in any way implying that there is any parliamentary wrong being done. Originally under this parliamentary system we had what is known as responsible government; that is,
The Address-Mr. Howard a government which was supposed to be responsible to parliament. Gradually that has been developed to the point where we now have parliament responsible to the government and not the other way around as it should be.
We have 23 hon. members of this house who are members of the cabinet and who in effect run practically every phase of our parliamentary discussion, debates and decisions. I do not think we can assume for a moment that in every government the members of that government represent the brightest people in the House of Commons because, as we know, to a degree political consideration is given to the selection of cabinet ministers in order that they may be representative of provinces across the nation.
In think we can offer a number of suggestions for the operation of this house in the consideration of its business which would give the opportunity to parliament to draw upon the best brains in the house and, give an opportunity for members to freely express their ideas and to vote freely on individual matters. In the first instance I feel there are far too many things that are classified as being want of confidence or indicating a lack of confidence in the government. If we were to confine what is or what is not a want of confidence to the motion we are now considering, to the budget debate and to the six supply motions there would be adequate opportunity for those in opposition to express by amendment their feelings with respect to what they feel the government has failed to do and in what this house should express its confidence.
When it comes to legislation and considering the laws that are to be applied to the Canadian people these, I think, should be debated freely and the votes taken on them should be allowed to be free votes so there would be provided freedom for the crossing of party lines. In that way individual government backbenchers would not feel required to support a piece of legislation merely because it had been introduced by a cabinet minister belonging to their own party.
I feel there should be far more reference of legislation to committees of the house where also free discussion and free votes should be allowed and dictation by party not imposed on members participating in the sittings of the committee. In addition, this would allow any interested citizen of Canada who cannot now appear before parliament itself the opportunity of appearing before the committee to express his ideas and thoughts on the legislation. As a result of all this I am sure we would be able to develop and enact legislation which would be to a far

The Address-Mr. Howard greater extent than is now possible legislation enacted in the interests of the Canadian people based upon the freely allowed expression of opinion and free votes of hon. members of this House of Commons.
The question of private members' bills must also be considered in a discussion of this kind. We have notification of a number of such bills on the order paper at this time. These private members' bills are representative of each political philosophy that exists in the house. I hope that this session we will not follow the practice we have in past sessions of talking out private members' bills and not allowing the house the opportunity of voting "Yes" or "No" on the idea embodied in the bills drafted by private members. We should be sufficiently conscientious to allow votes to be taken on these bills which again should be referred to standing committees for full discussion.
Motions fall into the same category as do private bills as being an expression of opinion on the part of an hon. member of this house and a free vote should be taken on the motions introduced by individual private members. These should not be talked out. The government that now controls the operation of parliament should either publicly, by saying so in the house or privately in the secret back room where they hold caucuses, reach the decision to allow this type of free expression to take place. A government sponsored bill which met amendment in committee stage or which even met defeat by free vote of hon. members of this house would not curtail the length of time the government would have in office. The government would not need to be afraid of having to call a new election nor would the government be defeated every time a piece of legislation was freely voted upon.
There are probably two bad features to the proposals I have advanced, neither one of which in my opinion is sufficiently valid to negate my proposals. One such feature is that if these proposals were put into effect they would represent an invasion of the present cabinet control over our parliamentary functions and, secondly, the adoption of the proposals would upset ministerial ego.
I believe it was two days ago that an announcement was made by a very large private corporation in this nation, namely the Aluminum Company of Canada, to the effect that it was not going to participate in selling for export to China an order for 2,000 long tons of aluminum. A question about this matter was put to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and he replied to it. The answer is to be found in yesterday's Hansard. It is to the effect that as far as he

knows no outside or foreign influence has been exerted upon the Aluminum Company of Canada in deciding whether they would sell this particular block of aluminum to China. I am going to suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not make an extensive enough investigation, or he has been ill-informed about this matter. I think it is quite evident that the Aluminum Company of Canada has certainly been dictated to by forces outside of this nation in its decision not to sell this particular amount of aluminum.
Alcan made reference to the fact that the decision had been made because it might lose some of its present customers if it sold to China. Let us look and see what nations are considered to be some of its customers. One of the largest purchasers of aluminum in Canada is in the United Kingdom. In the 11-month period ended November of last year we sold $63,500,000 worth of aluminum ingots to the United Kingdom, and we ask, was it United Kingdom influence, was it the United Kingdom market that Alcan was afraid they might lose if they sold aluminum to a country under communist domination? I think we can be fairly certain that since the United Kingdom has extended diplomatic recognition to China it would not declare that if Alcan sold aluminum to China it would lose any of its markets in the United Kingdom. We also know that the United Kingdom imported aluminum from Russia, another communist country, at a price which was lower than that at which Alcan sells aluminum. Therefore, the concern of the United Kingdom is not so much that of buying from Alcan or from anybody else but in buying where they can get the best possible price.
West Germany bought $12,500,000 worth of aluminum during the same period of time, which is a minor amount compared with that bought by the United Kingdom and by the United States. United States purchases amounted to $82,200,000 during that same period. The United States and the United Kingdom are by far the two largest purchasers of aluminum from the Aluminum Company of Canada. Their purchases amounted to something in the neighbourhood of 85 per cent or better of the exports of aluminum from Canada. But we must think in terms of the United States as to whether or not that was the influential body outside of Canada that had an effect upon Alcan in its decision not to sell.
Let us look and see who are on the board of directors of this company which claims to have no ties with the Aluminum Company of America. We find that Aluminum Limited, the holding company, owns the Aluminum Company of Canada. One-half of the board

of directors consists of American citizens and have their addresses listed in such places as Westport, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Boston, Washington and New York. Incidentally, there is another chap on the board who is well-known to Canadian parliamentary life, namely the Right Hon. C. D. Howe. Therefore, certainly, United States influence has been used against Alcan. Whether it be economic or political intimidation, that is another matter but in essence it was United States influence which disallowed this potential sale of aluminum to another country. That, of course, was admitted by officials of the Aluminum Company of Canada, as reported in yesterday morning's Globe and Mail. Mr. Duncan Campbell, the spokesman for Alcan, said, and I quote:
You know what the attitude of Americans is on sales to Red China.
He was obviously indicating that it was United States interference in one form or another that prevented the Canadian company from selling this particular commodity to another country at a time when we know how much we need to expand our exports for a variety of reasons.
Let us analyse what this potential sale would have meant had it been consummated. There is first the possibility of expanding our markets for aluminum which, as we know, has been declining over the past number of months to the point, incidentally, where the Aluminum Company of Canada is now operating at about 65 per cent of capacity. There is the question of markets and the effect the sale would have had upon employment in the aluminum smelters in Canada which have been slowly, month by month, laying off production employees. That one sale would have meant approximately $1 million, or the equal of the total sales we have made during the past year to India and to Hong Kong. It would have amounted to three times what they have sold to New Zealand in that year and five times what they sold to the Argentine. It would have almost equalled what we sold to South Africa and would have compared favourably with what we have sold to other countries during the past year.
We have the question of employment to consider. Within the last year and a half the Aluminum Company of Canada has been following a policy of curtailment of production, and a discontinuance of plant expansion, all of which is connected with their laying off of employees, thereby adding to the unemployed rolls of our nation. In Kitimat, which is in the constituency which I have the privilege to represent here, about a year and a half ago the Aluminum Company of Canada suddenly overnight decided that they were not going to proceed with any further
The Address-Mr. Howard expansion and laid off more than 1,500 construction employees, thereby wreaking havoc upon those construction workers and their families, many of whom had moved to Kitimat because the Aluminum Company of Canada told them that it was a 10-year project and said so just a few months before they laid them off. There has been a steady reduction in production, and there was a recent announcement that another 10 per cent reduction in production by the Aluminum Company would take place. This has had an effect in Kitimat, Arvida and Isle Maligne and throughout the Alcan empire. Approximately 700 employees are being affected by this recent reduction.
Apart from the economic results that that sale would have had on Canada, apart from the market question, apart from its effect upon employment, there is another phase which we should consider also, namely the political results. Some time ago this government saw fit to send out trade commissioners from Hong Kong into the mainland of China to discover what the trading potentials were or what markets were there. Since the government has said over the past months that it is concerned with expanding trade it should also look at this from the point of view of its political impact on the world. We know that Russia has been able in the past year to offer aluminum on the world market at prices lower than those at which the Aluminum Company of Canada, Alcoa, Reynolds and others are selling aluminum. We also know that Russia did not offer to sell aluminum to China at those prices. I am sure we can sense the division in the unity which has existed between the Soviet union and China and which, if present developments continue, will divide those two nations politically even more.
Apart from the immediate market question, apart from the immediate employment picture, here was an opportunity for the Aluminum Company of Canada to do something on behalf of world peace by assisting in widening the division between the Soviet union and China and attempting to draw the Chinese nation closer to the western world politically if that nation has not gone too far the other way. It is certainly one aspect which should have been taken into consideration.
Yesterday I posed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce which was not answered because of a statement by the Speaker that it probably was not the time and place to pose such an all-embracing question, but I shall ask it again. Not only from this decision of the Aluminum Company but from decisions of other private corporations in Canada, some of whom are direct subsidiaries of United States corporations, it

Having in mind the words and phrases spilled all over the country by the government about wanting to expand trade it would appear that there is ample room among the various agencies of government for the establishment of an export or import-export board, whatever you want to call it, part of whose function would be to purchase from the company concerned and make the sale to the country wanting to buy the aluminum. If we had had such a board it certainly could have played a part in the situation which developed the other day with respect to the Aluminum Company and the sale to China. Certainly as a government agency established by the authority of parliament and representing the views of the Canadian people it would have been in a position to take the Aluminum Company of Canada off the hook, having in mind that company's fears of some sort of retaliation against it by United States interests if it should make this sale. I certainly hope that the time will come when we will have such a board or agency which, in addition to other questions of trade, will be able to deal with similar situations should they arise in the future in order to ensure that our markets are expanded, that employment possibilities are increased in Canada and perhaps assist in the political sphere by promoting a somewhat more sensible approach among nations towards the common goal of world peace.
I should like to say a few words about an important question that was debated at some length in the first session I was here, 1957, was debated again in the last session, and which appears to be going to receive adequate discussion and debate this session. I made some slight reference to unemployment in discussing the question of the Aluminum Company of Canada and the proposed sale to China. We have listened to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on a number of occasions, and on each occasion it has seemed to me that these gentlemen appear to be more concerned with statistics than they are with people. Every time the Minister of Labour has an opportunity to discuss unemployment he mentions statistics. He does not mention the impact that unemployment has on people. He does not mention the sorrow and suffering of individual families. I think the Minister of Labour has

probably been seduced by the statistics compiled for him and has forgotten entirely the unemployed people who are involved in the compilation of such statistics. I do not want to get into the realm of the different sets of figures used by the minister and others and the question of which set is correct and which is not, which one is incomplete because it does not contain certain types of workers and which one is more than complete because it contains people who are not unemployed. By doing so I would be allowing myself to become involved in figures in the same way as the Minister of Labour who is concerned solely with what the graphs show and forgets entirely that it is men and women who are affected.
In Vancouver, for instance, there are approximately 11,000 to 12,000 unemployed people at the moment who cannot qualify for unemployment insurance because they were not even able to get sufficient work during the past year to qualify for the benefits paid. Because of the failure of the government at the last session to carry out its throne speech promises-never mind its election promises-we have these 11,000 to 12,000 people in Vancouver who could not secure enough work in the last year to accumulate enough contributions even to draw the pitifully small amount paid by way of unemployment insurance.
I grew up in Vancouver around 1937 and for the first time that I can remember there are bread lines and soup kitchens. To my personal knowledge this condition has not existed for many years. The fact that there are bread lines and soup kitchens in Vancouver is certainly not the fault of the hundreds of people who have to stand and wait for hours for a sandwich that some charitable organization is able to provide. It is certainly not their fault that they do not have sufficient money unless they had money and spent their savings hoping that prosperity was just around the corner, in accordance with the Prime Minister's foolish suggestion that we should spend our way to prosperity.
The Minister of Labour forgets or maybe he does not even know of the situation I encountered personally in Prince George last fall. Prince George is in the constituency of my neighbour and friend from Cariboo. It is the central location for employment in the lumbering, construction and logging industries for the entire north central portion of British Columbia. Many loggers, sawmill workers and construction workers go to Prince George in the hope of finding employment there or being sent to a job somewhere out of the city.

In the latter part of October I was in Prince George for a few days and I met two friends of mine I had known in the logging industry and with whom I had worked. They had been sleeping in parked cars in parking lots for a whole week because they could not get work, there was no place for them to stay and they had not had sufficient work last summer to entitle them to unemployment insurance benefits. There was no charitable organization there to provide even a soup kitchen or bread line.
It is that sort of thing that goes into making up these statistics. It would do the Minister of Labour and the rest of his colleagues in the cabinet, who have been so blinded by this graph they have been talking about, a lot of good to go out and stand in a breadline once in a while.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-While Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the motion to adopt the speech from the throne. May I also say it is a pleasure to be back in this chamber presided over so pleasantly by a witty and able speaker.
Since I was in this house last, I have spent considerable time in my riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador and covered most of that quite extensive district. I was as far north as Nain and in one respect the far north was better than the southern districts for the fishery was better than average in northern Labrador while it was a total failure elsewhere. Unfortunately there are comparatively few fishermen in this area, the great bulk of them being on the island of Newfoundland where the fishery was very poor.
There is one point I should like to mention in this respect. There is a small but locally important sea trout fishery in this area. I am told that the smoked sea trout from Nain is one of the great delicacies in food.

Unfortunately there have been difficulties in transportation. Perhaps if the C.N.R. boat which operates in these waters had a small refrigeration unit on board it might be possible to ship more of the fish to Goose Bay where it should find a ready market. Goose Bay, as hon. gentlemen know, is the site of a large and famous airport and is relatively populous.
The principal needs of southern Labrador from the federal standpoint are still communications and marine works. Some wharves and slipways are needed and air strips are badly required among other places at Cartwright, Port Hope, Simpson and Hopedale. The provincial department of highways have constructed two air strips at Nain and North West River and some further work may be needed, particularly on the latter. An air strip is also being constructed in St. Anthony by the provincial department of highways. These air strips are designed to fill the great need which exists during the period of freeze-up and break-up.
The provincial department of health operates planes for the Grenfell mission. These planes operate on floats in summer and skis in winter. But there are the periods of freeze-up and break-up, when there is too much ice and slob for floats and not enough firm ice for skis, when these planes are grounded. During these periods air strips are invaluable in these northern areas where the plane is often the instrument of life. During the fall before last eleven people died in Nain because the plane could not land with medical aid. More air strips are required to prevent recurrence of such tragedies.
Another need is for additional radio telephones. Progress has been made in this respect but there are still places which are completely isolated when winter locks up the Labrador. Small radio telephone sets can summon a doctor in time of need.
At the present time the C.B.C. operates a television station at Goose Bay but it is of low power and some increase is desirable to assure better reception at North West River some 16 miles away. The R.C.A.F. operates a radio station and within its limits gives good service. There is some desire for the C.B.C. to operate a radio station giving a broader coverage. A radio station in the St. Anthony and Battle Harbour areas to serve the Labrador is also desirable and I trust this matter will receive sympathetic attention.
However, the principal matter which I wish to stress in these remarks is the serious situation in which our fishermen find themselves.
A large proportion of the fishermen of Newfoundland live in my constituency and I might say that what applies to them applies
The Address-Mr. Granger generally throughout the province. The cod fishery is still the basic industry of our province. It is the historic industry of Newfoundland and it has had historic problems. But these problems were aggravated last year when economic disaster struck and the fishery failed. There were just no fish. With the almost sole exception of northern Labrador the fishery was practically a total failure. This was certainly true of the northeast coast much of which I visited personally. I travelled from place to place where the total catch was but a fraction of what it usually is and when some fish did appear there was no bait. This was doubly devastating. As there was no alternative employment the result was inevitable. Hardship and want occurred and this was followed by the toughest winter that many fine, independent fishermen have experienced for many years and this, of course, through no fault of their own.
The inevitable plight of Newfoundland fishermen was, of course, foreseen.
On October 21, 1958, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) as follows:
I have recently returned from a visit to my constituency where I have found that the failure of the cod fishery which is the mainstay of more than half the population of the northeast coast of Newfoundland is of even more serious proportions than earlier reports had led me to expect.
I should estimate that, because the fish were scarce and because bait was even scarcer, up to two-thids of the full-time fishermen will not have enough stamps to entitle them to unemployment insurance which alone saved a serious situation last winter.
In a normal year, even with a failure of the fishery, many of the fishermen would be able to supplement their incomes with earnings from work in the woods, but owing to the recession in the pulp and paper industry, there is little or no woods work in most areas in Newfoundland.
It is no exaggeration to say that half the fishermen on the northeast coast of Newfoundland will be forced to go on relief in the coming winter unless action is taken by the federal government to treat this failure of the cod fishery as an emergency situation calling for action similar to that taken by the government to assist the prairie grain farmers who experienced a crop failure this year that is certainly no more serious for them than the "crop failure" in the cod fishery is to the fishermen of Newfoundland.
You will recall that on August 30 when you announced the intention of the government to ask parliament to vote $40 million of special assistance to the grain farmers you stated that your government's "concept" of a national policy is based on the belief that the national welfare demands positive action to meet the basic causes of distress and maladjustment in particular industries and regions."
The situation of the fishermen of Newfoundland this year calls urgently for positive action to meet acute distress in the fishing industry.
The simplest way to meet this problem would be for the government to use the agency of the unemployment insurance commission which has the necessary machinery and, through the commission

The Address-Mr. Granger to provide every full time fisherman with the minimum contributions to entitle him to unemployment insurance. This method would ensure that assistance went to those who actually had a failure of the fishery. The government could make a special contribution from the treasury to reimburse the fund for the full cost of these "crop failure" benefits to the fishermen. The federal fisheries officers have full records from which it would be easy to determine who were full-time fishermen.
I have referred only to the northeast coast of Newfoundland because that is the only area of which I have personal first-hand knowledge but obviously any national policy to meet the basic distress of the fishermen should be applied to the whole Atlantic region, including Gaspe and the Saguenay.
I am, therefore, sending a copy of this letter to all members of parliament from fishing constituencies in the Atlantic region as well as to the ministers of fisheries and labour and the minister from Newfoundland with a request for their support in this appeal to the government of our country to give treatment to the fishermen who have experienced a disastrous "crop failure" equal to that already given to the grain farmers of the prairies.
I cannot emphasize too strongly that the problem calls for an early statement of positive action by the federal government, if many thousands of fishermen are not to be driven to accept relief in order to provide for their families in the coming winter.
I quote this letter in full because it sets out a plan whereby assistance could have been granted to Newfoundland fishermen. In fact, I think I might safely say it was a constructive suggestion advancing an idea calculated to be helpful. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) replied on October 28 saying, and I quote:
The matter is being looked into thoroughly by my colleagues the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Fisheries to whom I have forwarded copies of your letter.
I might add that I wired the Prime Minister on October 27, supporting the letter I have just quoted. Actually, I sent the wire on the eve of his departure from Canada and he had the thoughtfulness and courtesy to acknowledge my telegram from London.
On December 1 the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate wrote the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) in connection with his letter to the Prime Minister and he said, and I quote the pertinent parts:
December 1, as you are aware, is the first day on which seasonal benefits can be paid under the unemployment insurance law and I am sure most of the fishermen who, through no fault of their own, cannot qualify for seasonal benefits will be greatly disappointed that no decision has yet been announced by the government about the suggestion for emergency "crop failure" benefits I made in my letter.
I am sure you realize, as I know the Minister of Fisheries who has been in Newfoundland does, that the need is urgent and that many fishermen have already been obliged to accept relief.
The method of meeting the problem suggested in my letter would be simple to administer and fair to the fishermen, but if the method is not acceptable to the government, I strongly urge that action be taken in some other way to meet this pressing need.

The Minister of Labour replied:
You may rest assured that every possible action will be taken to assist the Newfoundland fishermen.
I must say that I really believed assistance to the fishermen would be forthcoming. But as time went on faith began to wane. On January 8 I wired a query to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) and received the following reply:
You are aware community stage program proceeding several localities. In addition department public works has extensive winter work program in many areas. Fishermen also eligible work on federal-provincial road programs sponsored by northern affairs and national resources. All these projects will assist fishermen through work provided and lasting benefit of facilities.
This made me fear that no effective assistance would be forthcoming, except in a few places where it may be possible to get ahead with community stages during the winter. However, on Friday, January 16, I was encouraged again when the Prime Minister replied to the following question of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, as reported at page 16 of Hansard:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government is going to take any action to relieve the distress caused by the failure of the cod fishery in Newfoundland, about which he will recall I wrote him last October, and which he advised me the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Fisheries were looking into urgently?

The answer was:

I said, sir, no consideration is being given to reducing the 15 stamps that are required for seasonal benefits at the moment, and that includes everyone.
I share the feeling that fishermen of Newfoundland and Labrador have been wronged by neglect. There was no similar attitude on the part of the government toward the prairie farmers last summer. Certainly, a Canadian fisherman deserves the same assistance as a Canadian farmer. I did not know that there was a double standard for Canadians.
I have quoted heavily from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and while on this subject I should like to make this comment. The Minister of Labour asked a day or so ago what he did when he was in the government. I would like to reply that when he was a Liberal cabinet minister he obtained unemployment insurance for fishermen. It was also said that his suggestion contained in his

letter of October 21 to the Prime Minister came late. I can only say that it was made six days before the program of aid to municipalities was announced.
In fairness, I do not want to belittle what has been done by the federal government and in particular I would like to mention the program of community stage construction. Community stages will fill a real need. It has been experienced in the past that where small landing wharves were built in fishing settlements the wharf tended to be the focal point for fishing activities. So important did they become for the handling of nets and the processing of fish that when, as occasionally happens, one of these installations is wrecked by storm the fishery in that place is threatened.
The community stage is designed to fill this need even more efficiently. It has been increasingly expensive and difficult to get material for fishing premises and the community stage will provide much improved facilities for handling fish. It is an important evolutionary step and should contribute substantially to the preservation and improvement of the fisheries. I would also like to express my appreciation to the Minister of Fisheries for the interest he has taken in the bait situation in Newfoundland.
I have talked at length on what was needed and was not done. At this eleventh hour I want to appeal again to the government to reconsider their decision regarding special assistance to fishermen who, through no fault of their own, have not enough stamps to qualify for unemployment insurance. There are approximately 17,320 fishermen in Newfoundland and 880 in Labrador, a total of 18,200. The number of claimants for unemployment insurance on December 31, 1958, was 5,617, less than one-third. Fishermen are in need, are on relief, are unable to maintain their property. Last fall through personal visits I saw whole communities in a state of hopelessness and want. Independent people should not be condemned to relief because a freak of nature has ruined their harvest. Many fishermen will not be able to prepare properly for the fishery this spring. They will not have money to spend on necessary repairs to gear and boats. Direct assistance is needed and additional work provided during the spring months of April and May so that the fishermen of Newfoundland may be prepared for the coming voyage which I am sure we all hope will be a bountiful one.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I want to take this opportunity to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the
The Address-Mr. R. Muir hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) on their most excellent speeches in moving and seconding the address. I hope that one or two prominent front bench Liberals listened intently to the remarks of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet because they could learn a lesson from him. May I also join with other hon. members in extending my congratulations to the newly elected members of this house.
There are many points in the speech from the throne that could be discussed but I should like to mention one of them at the moment. I refer to freight rates. For my people, the people of the province of Nova Scotia generally and, indeed, for those in all the maritime provinces, one of the most encouraging aspects of the speech from the throne is that it discloses that the government will recommend action to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the recent 17 per cent horizontal increase in freight rates. Even more encouraging is the pledge of the government made in December to institute a full study of the entire transportation problem. We in the maritimes regard this investigation as a hopeful sign that the inequities in the freight rate structure, which have contributed in no small measure to the fact that our provinces have not marched with the quick step of the other provinces in industrial progress, may finally be removed.
Our whole economy revolves around our ability to get our natural resource products to the rich central Canadian market. Located as we are on the eastern extremity of the nation and separated by hundreds of miles, we have to rely on efficient transportation at a price which will permit us to produce and give us a fair return. With the rapidly rising increases in the cost of transportation we are finding it increasingly difficult to progress. The high cost of freight has prevented us from getting a better share of markets for coal and steel produced in Nova Scotia.
At this very moment Nova Scotians are pondering another stark reminder that it costs us too much to get our goods to market. I am referring to two things. The first is the announcement by A. V. Roe of Canada Limited that its subsidiary firm, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, will have to lay off 4,000 men from its coal mines for at least a month because of lack of orders, plus another 500 construction workers. The second is the decision of the A. V. Roe Company not to expand its steel making facilities in Sydney but instead to invest $20 million on a cold rolling mill near Montreal. One of the reasons is plain

The Address-Mr. R. Muir and simple. It is high transportation costs. We need government action to help to alleviate these problems but by the same token I feel that we should have the utmost co-operation from those who are involved in our industrial life. I repeat that we should have the utmost co-operation from those who are involved in our industrial life.
I stated on Tuesday last that to my mind the actions of the A. V. Roe Company since acquiring control of Dosco last year were questionable, and at this time I should like to elaborate on why I made a statement of that nature and why I should have these convictions. I feel that there are many thousands like me in Nova Scotia who hold the same convictions because of the action, or should I say lack of action, on the part of the new controllers of our destiny. There are 150,000 people in Nova Scotia dependent on this great corporation even for their very livelihood. It came to Nova Scotia with the deed of ownership to Dosco securely tucked in its pocket, with promises and assurances of better days. There were fears expressed in many quarters that the coal, steel, shipbuilding and railway car manufacturing industries would be carted off to the central provinces as has happened before under new ownership in the case of so many of our industries. But Avro spokesmen said that this was an unwarranted fear. In one of his official press releases Avro president Crawford Gordon said:
We have but one aim, to expand this Canadian enterprise so that it will be stronger, more enduring and more profitable to its shareholders and employees and, at the same time, contribute something strong, solid and substantial to the development of the Atlantic provinces and their people.
These are very fine words. This statement prompted Nova Scotia premier Robert L. Stanfield, after Avro's campaign for Dosco control had succeeded, to state:
You have stated your confidence in this area and your intention to develop Dosco as a maritime enterprise. We accept your assurances and we look forward to a happy association which will be beneficial to us and profitable to you. You realize, I am sure, that Dosco is not just an industry in the ordinary sense; it is the staff of life for many communities in Nova Scotia. It is something much more than just a matter of dollars and cents. I am sure that in assuming control of Dosco you have accepted in full the major responsibilities that go with that control.
But what have we found since that time? Despite its avowed policy of getting out and selling coal, enforced holidays were imposed on our miners last year. This came after a series of denials by company officials that any cut-backs would be necessary. The miners were asked to boost their production. This they did. What did they get in reward? Layoffs. Is it not a strange coincidence that these

lay-offs should occur right in the midst of the wage negotiations now going on?
At this point I should like to refer to the co-operation that has come from the coal miners of Nova Scotia. There has not been one strike in the coal mining fields of Nova Scotia since 1947. As I have said, the coal miners have co-operated in every way possible. They have maintained a hold-the-line policy as far as wages are concerned. They have certainly done their part.
To return to the corporation, despite its fervent pledge to contribute something strong, solid and substantial to the development of the Atlantic provinces and their people, Avro took a decision to erect a $20 million steel plant outside Montreal. What about its Sydney steel plant? We are told that it will benefit in that it will be asked to supply the raw steel for the finishing plant in Montreal, But will the Sydney plant be called upon to supply that raw steel or will it be acquired from other steel mills closer to the plant at Montreal? I have reason to believe it will be some time after the Montreal mill is opened, a long time at that, before Sydney's plant will supply the new gigantic mill in Montreal.
Now we are faced with another major lay-off in our coal industry. This seems to Nova Scotians to be out of keeping with the professed determination of Avro to contribute something strong, solid and substantial to the development of the Atlantic provinces and their people.
Mr. Speaker, Avro spokesmen have been dealing Nova Scotians a continuous hand of conflicting statements. "We want to progress", they say, and then they lay off our workers. "We will not do anything to hurt the maritime economy", they say, and then they shift the heart of their steel making industry from Sydney to Montreal. Nova Scotians have begun to hold new fears and doubts about the intentions of the Avro organization. The only expansion proposed by this company is a cold rolling mill near Montreal.
In addition to this, a series of company statements issued in recent months make it apparent that the company entertains long-range plans for a basic steel plant on adjacent property. If this comes to pass, then the future of Sydney as a major steel production centre will not be bright. When blast furnaces join the Montreal units to provide fully integrated operations in central Canada, what will happen to Sydney?
The Avro organization was born and has been nurtured on government contracts. The company has grown as a result of these government orders to become one of the giants of Canadian industry. Is it unreasonable, then,
*
28S

to expect that such a company should be among the first to gear its productive power to the wishes of the government and the public? Is it unreasonable to ask Avro to develop maritime economy and contribute towards the decentralization of industry?
It is my view, and one that is shared by many Nova Scotians, that the government has a right to expect co-operation from Avro and other companies that have thrived on government work. Since this government took office in 1957, it has offered material assistance to Avro and its subsidiary, Dosco. On August 22, 1957, additional assistance over and above the subvention provided on movements of all Nova Scotia coal, was authorized on shipments of coal from the Springhill collieries. On January 15, 1958, the House of Commons passed the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. Amongst other things, this act authorized the payment by the government of Canada of a subvention on coal mined in eastern Canada and used in the four Atlantic provinces in the production of electric power by steam driven generators. This was to help stabilize and ultimately increase the market for coal.
Again on February 18, 1958, the cabinet issued a directive to government departments that Canadian coal be used in all government coal-burning installations where the laid-down cost of such coal did not exceed the competitive cost of other coals by more than 20 per cent. Again on April 14, 1958, the subvention policy was revamped raising the amount of government assistance on transportation of Nova Scotia coal to Ontario and western Quebec from 45 per cent of freight rates to 60 per cent; offers were made to the company of assistance of $4 per ton on movements of coal from Nova Scotia to Europe, and on the same day, the special assistance to the Springhill mines was extended to March 31, 1959. Of course, this does not apply to Springhill mines at this time because of the disaster that occurred there.
I join with my colleague, the member for Cumberland, in extending to those brave people my sincere sympathy. Mere words of mine, in fact mere words of anyone are not any use to people who have gone through what these people have gone through. Having worked in the coal mines myself, and having come through a gas explosion in a coal mine, I know in a very small, and very minute way what some of these men have gone through.
On June 10, 1958, an order in council was approved granting an additional 55 cents per ton subvention assistance to permit the sale of approximately 175,000 tons of Nova Scotia coal in Belleville, Ontario. Again, on June 27, 1958, the federal government broadened
The Address-Mr. R. Muir the base of its subvention payment schedule so as to include amongst the cost audit items to be determined by the comptroller of the treasury the amount of the insurance, stockpile and interest charges on excess coal stockpiled in 1958. It has been estimated the additional cost will be $500,000. The provincial government of Nova Scotia assisted in this measure by agreeing to contribute one-fifth of the cost, and the federal government will contribute the balance.
Another indication of assistance is the fact that on August 18, 1958 parliament accepted a government measure granting the Dominion Coal Company a five-year recess in payment of a $5,198,242 loan which it received from the federal government to assist in the cost of mechanization of the mines. I understand that the federal cabinet now has under consideration the recommendations of the dominion coal board concerning the industry's application, made in December, for increased subventions which, it is claimed, will be needed to penetrate the heavy consuming Ontario power production market. I mentioned December as the time when these submissions were made, in order to make it clear, it was not three months ago as was noted in the Halifax newspaper recently in a statement made by a former member of the dominion coal board. I feel that in making a statement of that nature he took advantage of a situation such as this, when people are going to suffer, to make a statement for political purposes. However, I could be wrong. He is only the past president of the provincial Liberal association.

speechtext: That is hardly worthy of the rest of your very good speech.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall ignore that comment, as I usually have to do in so far as comments by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill' are concerned. I should like him to go back to his newspaper if he does not wish to listen to me.
It is my hope, and certainly the hope of all Nova Scotians-the hon. member may not even be interested in our coal miners, so it might be better if he did read his newspaper -that the government will see its way clear to providing, within the framework of national and international policies, favourable action on the application in order to prevent further lay-offs and possibly reduce the length of the lay-off currently proposed by the company. I urge this sincerely and wholeheartedly, although I do know that in the short period this government has been in power it has certainly done its part.

The Address-Mr. R. Muir
In conclusion, I should like to refer to the statement of Sir Thomas Sopwith, chairman of the Hawker Siddeley group which controls Avro, made at the annual meeting. I quote:
One final word on Canada. Your interests there are in good hands, with the company being well and efficiently managed by a team of energetic young and capable Canadians. The future of Canada is bright and glowing with promise. Because of the spread and the diversification of our holdings in Canada, it is our belief, that your company is well placed to grow and to prosper with Canada itself.
Does this mean that we in the maritimes will share in this growth and prosperity to which he refers, or does it mean more closed mines and possibly a closed steel plant? Does this mean a new series of conflicting statements which are damaging to the morale of the people who live in the maritimes? Does this mean that their boasting in a recent issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald about their assets really indicates that Dosco is going bankrupt? Does this mean that the company will encourage its salesmen to get out and try to sell more coal, or does it mean we will be importing American coal into the maritimes to the very back door of our own coal mines? Does it mean, perhaps, that the proposed march on Ottawa by the coal miners of Nova Scotia should be diverted to the company's head office in Montreal or even to London-although I thought we were no longer colonials? Does this mean that despite the utmost government co-operation which has been forthcoming Avro will continue to mislead many breadwinners who are dependent on the company for a livelihood? Does it mean that, at long last, the people of Nova Scotia can rely on the word of this gigantic corporation and place their faith in it? We must remember that faith without works is dead. We have not seen much evidence of the work, so it is rather difficult for the people of the maritimes to have faith.
This gigantic corporation has the future destiny of Nova Scotians in the palm of its hand. It is gigantic. It appears that the more gigantic a corporation becomes, the more ruthless it can be. I am sure that all members in this house and all Canadians who contribute through taxation to the development of industry are awaiting the answers to these and many other questions.

speechtext:
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I too should like to add my congratulations to those which have been expressed to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was particularly proud of my colleague, the hon. member for Provencher, for his address on agriculture. It certainly should show this house that we in the west have an extremely able spokesman for agriculture.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet on his extremely able address on national unity particularly. I was greatly interested in listening to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) the other day when he made some statements with regard to the Liberal party and national unity. I do not know whether he will fool anybody in eastern Canada with that kind of talk but we in the west have realized for the last 20 years how the Liberal party went about national unity. They split us into so many pieces that we could not possibly have an effective voice in the working of this country. As I have said, my colleague, in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, made some pertinent remarks with regard to the agricultural situation in western Canada particularly. I should just like to make some comment in that regard.
We all know that for the first time we have an energetic government working to solve the problems of agriculture. For the first time we have a government which- has recognized that agriculture has problems. That is the first important step. As you listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) in today's debate, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will have realized two major

things. The first is that this government has gone a long way in implementing its national policies for agriculture. The second thing is that the Liberal party is completely barren of any policy on agriculture. We in western Canada who are dependent upon our trade and our export markets were highly pleased with the trip of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to the commonwealth countries and to the other nations of this world. Surely we have no better salesman in all of Canada than the Prime Minister.
I should like to add a word of thanks to the Minister of Agriculture for several things which have improved the lot of the small farmer in my constituency. First of all, the acreage payments were indeed a boon to these small farmers and meant a great deal. The change in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has made it possible, for the first time in 25 years, for those farmers in my constituency at least to qualify under these regulations.
Further, I should like to thank him for what he has done to have Johne's disease or paratuberculosis in cattle included in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, as I mentioned in a speech in the house last year.
The new agricultural subjects which the speech from the throne indicates will be brought forward in legislation at this session include the crop insurance program and the new credit arrangement for farmers. These are things which the farmers have been working for over the years. Under the previous regime nothing was done. The farmers were told, "We are not worried about
The Address-Mr. H. Horner you. We have you all split up amongst a bunch of splinter parties. You have not any effective voice. We are not even going to the bother of doing anything about it"; and they did not do so.
We are also happy in western Canada, as I am sure are people in all of Canada, that this government is going to bring forward a conservation program. Conservation is an important thing. It is important to conserve our land because that is our greatest natural resource. We must look after it.

VISIT TO THE SENATE BY MEMBERS OF THE CANADIAN PARLIAMENT EXTRACT FROM CONGRESSIONAL RECORD OF JANUARY 9, 1959
speechtext:
Mr. President, many of us have been looking forward to this day with great pleasure. Senators will recall that on August 8, 1958, the Senate adopted Senate Resolution 359 reading as follows:
Resolved, that the Senate committee on foreign relations shall establish a subcommittee for the purpose of exploring, with appropriate officials of the government of the United States and with members of the Canadian parliament, the desirability and feasibility of increased systematic discussion between legislators of the two countries on problems of common concern.
I shall read two sentences from the committee report of Senate Resolution 359 to indicate the motivation behind the resolution:
It was the feeling of the committee on foreign relations that an attempt should be undertaken to strengthen the bonds between the United States and its great neighbor, the commonwealth of Canada. In these critical times, it is of crucial importance that the friendship and understanding between our nations be deepened in every possible way.
Mr. President, this Senate resolution did not simply happen. For some years, members of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations and of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have been keenly aware of the special relationship between the United States and Canada and the useful results which might flow from increased contact between legislators of the two countries. In May, 1957 a report by Representative Frank M. Coffin and Representative Brooks Hays suggested that some form of parliamentary consultation between the two countries be established. In a speech at Wesleyan University on June 8, 1958, Prime Minister Diefenbaker referred to this concept. The subject was further discussed last July by the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States.
Pursuant to Senate Resolution 359, I was privileged to be named by Chairman Green of the Committee on Foreign Relations to be the chairman of a liaison committee. My colleagues on that committee are Senators Mansfield, Capehart, and Morse. Last September I went to Ottawa where I was joined by Senator Capehart and we had a preliminary discussion with members of the Canadian parliament, some of whom are here today. Later in September, Representative Brooks Hays and Representative Frank M. Coffin held similar discussions in Canada. As a result of these discussions it was determined that a delegation of members of the Canadian
parliament would come to Washington at this time. Acting Chairman Morgan of the House Foreign Affairs Committee has appointed a liaison committee composed of Representative Edna F. Kelly, chairman, and Representatives Frank Coffin, Walter H. Judd, and Chester E. Merrow.
Mr. President, this is in brief the background of the introduction which I am about to make. A delegation of most distinguished members of the Canadian parliament is now with us to continue the consultations begun in Canada last fall. Mr. President, I ask unanimous consent to insert in the record at this point in my remarks certain biographic information about the Canadian delegation.
Mr. President, it is indeed a high privilege to present to this body the Speaker of the Senate of Canada, the Hon. Mark Drouin. [Applause, Senators rising.]
Mr. President, it is also a high privilege to present to the Senate the Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada, the Hon. Roland Michener. [Applause, Senators rising.]
Speaker Drouin is accompanied by two of his colleagues, the Hon. Sydney John Smith and the Hon. William R. Brunt. [Applause, Senators rising.]
Speaker Michener of the House of Commons is accompanied by five of his colleagues, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the hon. Hazen Argue, the hon. William L. Houck, the hon. Richard D. Thrasher, and the hon. Erik Nielsen. [Applause, Senators rising.]
Mr. President, if the rules of the Senate permitted it, I would call attention to the fact that the wives of seven members of the Canadian delegation and the daughter of one member are in the gallery. [Applause.]
Mr. President, I know that other members of the Senate wish to pay their respects to our distinguished guests. I am happy to yield at this time for that purpose; and after they leave the floor, they will go to the office of the Vice President, where other Senators may meet them.

Mr. President, understanding and friendship are a two-way street. Out of friendship comes understanding, and out of understanding comes friendship; and of course, that process makes our relationship so pleasant and makes understanding so very easy.
Of course, our two countries have the common experience of Anglo-Saxon background and a common language; and out of that has come, over a long period of time, the felicity which makes you call us your neighbor, and makes us call you our neighbor.

speechtext:
Mr. President, I wish to say to our distinguished guests and friends that I am their neighbor; I live in North Dakota. I have had many delightful experiences in meeting citizens of Canada who have visited North Dakota.
Of course, I, in turn, like to visit Canada, both to enjoy my experiences there and
meetings with its fine citizens and to enjoy the fishing. In addition we have the benefit of the great Peace Garden.
I want to compliment our distinguished visitors for the fine way their government treated the farmers of Canada after World War I. Within a year Canada cancelled every seed and feed loan. But in North Dakota alone there were 34,000 farmers; and today our government still is charging 4,000 of them 6 per cent interest a year, and the result is that the interest amounts to a great deal more than the principal.
So when we meet in the Peace Garden and when our farmers join your farmers in celebrating, our farmers are very much distressed to find that they have not received from their government the fine treatment that your government has given to the farmers of Canada.
I join my colleagues in bidding you welcome. It is most delightful and indeed a very great pleasure to see you here.

speechtext:
Mr. President, I wish to say to our Canadian friends that I have the privilege of serving under the leadership of Senator Aiken, who is chairman of our so-called Canadian subcommittee of the Foreign Relations Committee, of which the Senator from Indiana  is also a member; and then I have the privilege of having them serve with me in my capacity as chairman of the subcommittee on Latin-American Affairs.
The message I would leave with our distinguished Canadian brothers is that in my opinion we have a comity of interest and obligations in respect to Latin America. I have said at meetings of the Foreign Relations Committee, and I wish to say now to our distinguished guests, that in my judgment Canada and the United States should proceed as brothers in the attempt to solve the relationships with Latin America, to the end that they may be improved and that there will be a better understanding throughout Latin America in regard to her two northern neighbors.
My conversations with members of the Canadian parliament in the past lead me to believe that you gentlemen share that point of view. Therefore, in my capacity as a member of Senator Aiken's subcommittee and as chairman of the Latin-American subcommittee, I invite you to join with us in a partnership arrangement, to the end that we may strengthen the policies toward Latin America on the part of both Canada and the United States.

speechtext:
Mr. President, I, too, would like to join my distinguished colleagues in a word of welcome to our dear friends, these distinguished members of the parliament of Canada. I represent in part the state of New York, a state with which they have many important relationships, both in the economic field, in social terms, and in governmental matters. I hazard the guess that they visit my state perhaps more than any other state in our nation.
Of course Canadians are always very welcome in New York, as they know. We count them as brothers, and we mean that very literally. Furthermore, the state of New York prides itself on its economic relations with Canada. Canada joins us in connection with the St. Lawrence Seaway and in connection with the use of the waters of the Niagara river and its tremendous power development and the great community of interest that exists between us.
I think I speak advisedly when I say that today our new Governor, Nelson Rockefeller, has very close to his heart the entire matter of United States-Canadian relations, particularly in terms of the interests of our own state; and as these gentlemen have experienced with our governors prior to Governor Rockefeller, I believe they will find a welcome hand, a warm understanding, and a spirit of great co-operation added to a spirit of new enterprise in terms of the government of the state of New York. I know I certainly bespeak the views of my colleague from New York, who does not happen to be on the floor at the moment.

speechtext:
Mr. President, I wish to join my colleagues in welcoming our neighbors from across the border, members of the parliament of Canada.
Because I represent, in part, the state which has perhaps the closest contact with the most Canadian provinces, since Montana borders on British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, and because I know something about the many problems which sometimes cause us trouble and difficulty, but never divide us, I am delighted that these members of the Canadian parliament are here to visit with us, to discuss these difficulties, and to arrive at common understandings.
I wish to commend the distinguished Senator from Vermont  for taking the

initiative in the establishment of this interparliamentary group, so to speak, and I wish to point out that he got the idea from Premier Diefenbaker, who, while visiting Trinity College, in Connecticut, made a speech to the effect that a liaison group of this kind would be in the best possible interest of both countries.
So I am delighted that these gentlemen are here. I hope this meeting is only the beginning of many similar meetings in the future; and 1 know that from them will come a better understanding, a better feeling, and an accentuation of the good will which has marked the relationships between our two countries, not only since both of our countries became independent, but even before then.

speechtext:
Mr. President, I wish to join my colleagues today in extending the warm hand of friendship and welcome to these distinguished members of the parliament of Canada.
It is my privilege to represent, in part, in this body the great state of Minnesota. Of course, Minnesota joins territorially and geographically the great country of Canada; and our relationships are cordial, friendly, and, indeed, helpful to both areas.
Likewise, we are at the end of the great St. Lawrence seaway. So that our relationships in the area of commerce with Canada are closer than ever. Many people from Minneapolis and St. Paul travel to Winnipeg, Canada, and many persons from Winnipeg come to the Twin Cities.
When I was mayor of Minneapolis, I visited Winnipeg, and the mayor of Winnipeg came to our area. Those relationships are very happy memories. But I believe now, as has been suggested today, we would do well to talk of the future, and resolve to solve our problems as good friends do, respecting the rights of each other, and making such accommodations as will provide for unity through understanding and mutual respect.
I join with the Senator from Vermont , and wish to commend him upon his worthy endeavors and leadership in establishing, on our part, this very fine example of co-operation between two great countries. I am looking forward to the coming days when we can be together again.
Mr. Case of South Dakota: Mr. President, will the Senator from Texas yield to me?

Welcome to Canadians by U.S. Senators
Mr. Case of South Dakota: I think probably I am one of the very few members of the U.S. Senate who found it convenient and desirable to go home last August by way of Canada. I live in South Dakota, but I went to New England, and, from lake Champlain, went to Canada. I visited Ottawa, and saw the government house, and some of the very fine and outstanding buildings there. In fact, it was my thought at the time that Ottawa was splendidly equipped to be the scene of international conferences and international groups, as it has been in the past. I am sure it will be in the future.
From there I went north, to Algonquin provincial park. I may say to my colleague from North Dakota that I saw a shorthorn cow which I thought was the largest cow I had ever seen. [Laughter.]
I have a picture of it. I am exhibiting it to my friends in South Dakota and saying, "Take a look at that, and do your best." We spent a few days at Huntsville, in the beautiful lake country of that area. It is magnificent. I was proud that it was a part of a country that is our friend, Canada.
You are most welcome here. I hope some of you will visit us in South Dakota.

subtopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY MEMBERS OF THE CANADIAN PARLIAMENT EXTRACT FROM CONGRESSIONAL RECORD OF JANUARY 9, 1959
speechtext:
Mr. President, as one of the representatives in the Senate from the state of Texas and as a member of the Senate Interstate and Foreign Commerce Committee, I want to join in these words of welcome to our friends, the members of the Canadian parliament with us in the Senate today. The Senate Interstate and Foreign Commerce Committee has no jurisdiction over legislation dealing with foreign relations but does have jurisdiction over laws relating to foreign commerce.
In the last session we had the privilege of passing two bills which furthered commerce between Canada and the United States. One of those bills extended the time during which a Canadian-owned steamship line may serve the 49th state by furnishing service between Alaska and the other 48 states. I think it is an anomaly that the only regular steamship service between Alaska and the other 48 states is furnished by a Canadian steamship line.
Many citizens from my state have been to Alaska. The only way they can get to Alaska overland is by going through Canada over the Alcan highway. The only transportation ties between our old 48 states and the new 49th state by land or water have been by 66968-9-19J
Canadian aid, either through using Canadian steamship service, or overland, across Canada itself. Such transportation bridge between our newest state, Alaska, and the older 48 states across the Dominion of Canada, serve to strengthen the ties of commerce and bonds of friendship that link our two nations and peoples.
In the last session of the Congress there also was passed a bill which permitted foreign-owned vessels-British and Canadian owned barges primarily-to use the inland waterways of the United States. Such laws deal with commerce, and not with treaties. They deal with people-to-people relations, further promoting the commercial relations of our two nations.
There is another phase of this subject in which our people are directly interested, and that is gas and oil lines from the great reserves in Canada to markets in the United States. More gas and oil pipelines have been projected.
Our friends will recall that during the dark days of World War II our war effort was crippled by the fact that so many ships were sunk by German submarines. The enemy at that time had only about one-eighth the number of submarines now possessed by countries behind the Iron Curtain.
In the event another such tragedy should befall us, the oil and gas pipelines which link these energy reserves with the industrial centres of our two nations would provide the means of furnishing fuel and energy to both of our countries, to help us survive in any assault which might possibly be made against us.
We want our Canadian friends to know we are appreciative of their co-operation. You have permitted the building of the D.E.W. line, the radar observation chain, in your northern territories, so that the first warning of attack on the United States or Canada will come from your territory. We are grateful to you for the great friendship and co-operation of your people in these endeavors.
I am glad to help welcome you to the floor of the U.S. Senate.

speechtext:
As the senior Senator from the state of Ohio, which is in physical contact with Canada except for lake Erie, I wish to extend a welcome to you in your visit to the United States. I believe I speak the will of the people of Ohio when I say to you we have recognized the mutual interdependence which exists between Canada and the United States.
I feel positive that the people of Ohio recognize that the things which hurt Canada will eventually hurt Ohio. We believe that as Canada grows stronger, the United States will grow stronger. We believe that if we grow weak, Canada will inevitably grow weak. We are neighbors standing shoulder to shoulder, lifted and dropped by every good thing or every bad thing that affects us.
As a member of the Senate, I should like to say to you that in my approach to my responsibilities with respect to Canada, I will constantly have in mind that anything imprudent which I did, prejudicially affecting your dominion, inevitably will affect my nation. I think I speak the thinking and the will of the citizens of Ohio when I deliver that message to you.

speechtext:
My friends from Canada, as a representative of a state bordering on lake Superior, a large part of which provides the southern line of Canada, and speaking also on behalf of the Senator who now occupies the Chair, the junior Senator from the state of Wisconsin , I bid you welcome. It is good to see some old acquaintances in this delegation, friends I made in connection with meetings of those interested in the St. Lawrence development. One I knew when attending sessions of the United Nations.
Canada has been of interest to me from the days when I was a boy and read the story of Evangeline. As I grew into manhood, I visited the cities of Quebec and Montreal. I travelled through the lake country and across the continent on the Canadian Pacific, up to Lake Louise and Banff, and on to the west coast. It seemed to me that God Almighty had created this continent to be one geographically, to be one in its political
approaches, although our governments were separate as nations, one in the religious approach of our people, and one in the economic approach to domestic and world problems.
I think it is a wonderful thing, gentlemen, that this exchange of members of parliamentary bodies has gotten underway to such a point that groups such as yours, who really are the ambassadors of good thinking and good living, visit their neighbors. It makes for the constructive building up of relationships in every direction. We welcome you, and may you begin today to have the time of your lives in the good old U.S.A.
